events.text: Something has happened to your voice. Since the spring every song you sing has all five notes of the old court scale in it at once: gung, low like a tiled roof; sang; gak; chi; u, high like water on a stone. The musicians of the capital have noticed. Three of them are camped on the ledge under your cliff with two zithers, a frame of stone chimes and a bamboo pipe each, and they have been tuning to you for nine days.

choices.text: Sing the scale for them slowly, one note at a time

effects.log: It takes all summer. By autumn every instrument in the court is tuned a hair flatter than it was, to a bird on a cliff, and the old music master swears that the Shao sounds right for the first time in his life.

choices.text: Sing the way you always sing, and let them catch what they can

effects.log: They catch about half. The half they catch goes into the court music for three hundred years. The half they miss is argued about by every music master since.

choices.text: Fly to another cliff. A voice is not an instrument

effects.log: They follow you for two cliffs and give up at the third. The youngest does not give up. That one comes back every spring for years, and sits on the ledge, and listens.

events.text: {npc}, the youngest of the musicians, has come back, spring after spring, with new pipes: twelve lengths of bamboo, cut from a grove that flowered and died. "From your own grove," {he} calls up the cliff. "Seed for you, pipes for me. The bamboo should get to sing once, after it feeds you."

choices.text: Sing into the pipes as {he} plays

mem.note: played twelve bamboo pipes to the Phoenix

effects.log: Twelve pipes and one bird. Down in the valley the farmers straighten up in the paddies and cannot say what they are hearing. {npc} plays until {his} lips split, and laughs.

choices.text: Sing one note over and over until {he} trims the pipe that is wrong

mem.note: was taught the true note by a bird

ok.log: The seventh pipe was a shaving too long. {npc} trims it with a knife, plays it, and sits down on the ledge as if {he} had been struck.

fail.log: {npc} trims the wrong pipe, then the right one, then the wrong one again. By dusk the set is shorter by a hand and exactly in tune. Neither of you mentions how.

choices.text: Tell {him} to play them for the villages, not for a bird

effects.log: {npc} looks up at the cliff for a long time, then goes down the mountain with the pipes. For years the market towns of the south hear twelve bamboo pipes at harvest, and never know what they were tuned to.

events.text: {npc} is old now, and the court has sent {him} away: the new ruler below likes loud music, drums and horns, and says the old pipes sound like a sick bird. Every evening {he} climbs the hill under your cliff with the twelve bamboo pipes and plays them to nobody.

choices.text: Come down, and sing with {him} once, in sight of the village

mem.note: sang with the Phoenix in sight of the village

effects.log: Half the village sees it: the dismissed old musician on the hill, and the five-coloured bird standing beside {him} in the dusk, singing the part the pipes cannot reach. The court hears of it within a week, and looks foolish for a generation.

choices.text: Sing from the cliff, so only {he} knows

mem.note: heard the Phoenix answer every evening

effects.log: Every evening the pipes, and every evening an answer from the cliff. {npc} plays until {he} cannot climb the hill, and then from the doorway, and you answer the doorway.

choices.text: Fly over the court at its next feast and sing the old scale over the drums

effects.log: Every drum in the hall goes slightly out of tune with you, at once. The ruler laughs it off. The musicians do not, and by spring three of them have walked to the hill under your cliff with their own pipes.

events.text: The music masters of two kingdoms have quarrelled for a century over whose scale is the true one, and they have both sent envoys to your cliff with gifts of millet, which you do not eat, and the same question: which of us sings like the Phoenix?

choices.text: Sing both scales, one after the other, and fly away

effects.log: Both envoys go home certain that you sang their scale first. The quarrel lasts another century, more politely, and the music is better on both sides for it.

choices.text: Tell them you judge no one, and sing nothing

effects.log: The envoys wait a month. The one who waits longer goes home and tells the court that the Phoenix's silence was in their scale. Nobody can disprove it.

choices.text: Sing the note the two scales share, only that one, for a whole day

ok.log: One note, all day. By evening the two envoys are sitting on the same rock, and by the next year their courts are sending each other musicians instead of envoys.

fail.log: Each envoy writes the note down in their own notation, and each notation proves, to its own court, that you favour them. You leave them to it.

events.text: The old song says the phoenixes reach up to heaven. Nobody ever said how. This morning your mate simply keeps flying: up the paulownia slope, over the ridge, past the height where the larks give up, up the column of light the sun lays on the mist, and looks back at you from very high, as if to ask whether you are coming.

choices.text: Follow, wing to wing

effects.log: You climb the light together until the land is a map and then a colour and then nothing. Your breath goes thin, then strange, then easy. The two shadows you cast fall on cloud now, not on water.

choices.text: Race them up the light

effects.log: You pass them at the height of the cranes and they pass you at the height of the wind. Nobody wins. At the top you are both too out of breath to argue about it, which is new.

choices.text: Call them back down: the land below has a reign to watch

effects.log: They come down, slowly, and sit on the branch beside you, and say nothing for a season. Next spring, without a word, you are the one who keeps flying, and they follow.

events.text: You sing both halves of the song at dawn on the high ridge, as you have every dawn since your mate was lost, and this morning the second half does not come back off the mountains. It goes up. The column of light the sun lays on the mist is carrying it, and a voice in you that is not quite yours says: follow it.

choices.text: Follow your own song up the light

effects.log: You climb alone, singing the part your mate used to sing so you have something to fly toward. At the height where the larks give up, you could swear there are two shadows on the cloud below you. There are not. You keep singing.

choices.text: Stay on the ridge one more year, for the branch where they last sat

effects.log: One more year on the ridge. The light waits, the way light does. When you finally go up it, the paulownia below lets go of one leaf, as if it were waving.

events.text: At the top of the light there is a door, if a door can be made of cloud: two pillars of white weather and a lintel of mist, and beyond it a blue too deep to have a name. Across the threshold run hoofprints, each one a small pool of light, so lightly set down that the cloud is not even bent. Something walked here that would not crush an ant.

choices.text: Follow the hoofprints through the door

effects.log: The prints lead a long way and then stop, at the edge of nothing, as if whatever made them simply stood still to think. You stand in its place. You can see every land under heaven from here, and you understand that it was looking for you.

choices.text: Wait on the threshold to be asked in

effects.log: You wait three years on the threshold. Nobody asks. On the morning of the fourth a fresh line of hoofprints has appeared, coming toward the door and stopping a respectful distance from you, as if whatever made them was also waiting to be asked.

choices.text: Go back down. Heaven can come to you

effects.log: You fly down the light. Behind you, on the threshold, a line of hoofprints appears and follows you as far as the door, and stops, and you have the strong feeling that something is smiling.

events.text: Word from the Four Spirits, and it comes the way such word comes: one morning every bird on your mountain lands facing the same way, south and up, and stays there. The hundred birds were kept from scattering by you. Now something is keeping you. The message is not in words. It is: come and be read.

choices.text: Go at once

effects.log: You go at once. The birds turn and watch you out of sight, and then, for the first time in a century, they scatter, as birds should.

choices.text: Set the land below in order first: one more season of watching

effects.log: One season more over the capital, the granaries, the prisons, the springs. Whatever you are asked up there, you will at least know what is true down here.

choices.text: Ask your mate whether you should go

effects.log: "We," your mate says, which is the whole answer.

events.text: Up here at the edge of heaven the wind has no smell. No smoke, no paddy mud, no bamboo, no millet. You catch yourself, one morning, missing millet: not wanting to eat it, only missing the smell of the farmyards it came from, and the hands that threw it.

choices.text: Go down to the farmyards for a season, and come back

effects.log: A season low over the farmyards, among the hens and the drying peppers and the children. You eat nothing there. You come back up the light smelling of woodsmoke, and the edge of heaven seems less empty.

choices.text: Stay. The edge of heaven is where you are now

effects.log: You stay. The missing does not stop, but it changes, the way a scar changes, and in a century it is only a fondness.

events.text: It takes a tortoise eleven years to climb into the sky, and this one has done it without stopping: a black tortoise as big as a threshing floor, a black serpent coiled round its shell, a long writing brush tucked under the serpent's coils, both heads talking at once. The Black Tortoise, which keeps the record. "The Four Spirits," says the tortoise. "Will hear your record," says the serpent. "Before the fourth seat is filled," they finish together. "Bring every reign. We already know them."
events.arc: The Court of the Four Spirits

choices.text: Bow to the Tortoise

effects.log: The tortoise approves. The serpent says it has seen better bows, from a dragon, once. They argue about which dragon for the rest of the afternoon, and you understand that this is how the Tortoise does everything.

choices.text: Ask why the Four Spirits need a record at all

effects.log: "The guardians hold the four walls of the sky," says the serpent. "The spirits hold nothing," says the tortoise. "They only come. So everything depends on where they came," they finish, "and for whom." At their age it seems obvious.

choices.text: Tell them your record is written on your own body

effects.log: "It is," says the tortoise mildly, looking at the patterns on your head and wings and back and breast and belly, and the dark places between them. The serpent laughs, a dry sound like ice cracking on a river.

events.text: The Court of the Four Spirits is the same cloud terrace among the stars where the four directions hold their council, on the nights the directions are not sitting. At its edges a blue storm and a white frost lean in to watch, the guardians of the east and the west, who are not spirits and know it. In the centre a coil of gold cloud lies with its eyes shut: the Yellow Dragon, which listens with the patience of farmland. And on the terrace, walking round you in a slow circle without bending the cloud it walks on, is the Qilin, which asks the questions.
events.arc: The Court of the Four Spirits

choices.text: Stand still and let it walk round you

effects.log: Three times round, very slowly. It has one horn, and the horn is tipped with flesh, so that it can wound nothing. It looks at your patterns one by one, the way a farmer reads a sky. Then it stops in front of you and asks its first question.

choices.text: Walk the circle with it, matching its steps

effects.log: You walk in a measured dance, the one you came down into courtyards with. The Qilin looks sideways at you, and its step changes very slightly to meet yours. The Yellow Dragon opens one eye.

events.text: The Qilin's first question, in a voice like rain on a thatched roof: "Every reign you came for. Which of them did not deserve you?" The serpent unrolls the inside of the shell. The tortoise has the brush ready. Nobody on the terrace pretends not to know the answer.
events.arc: The Court of the Four Spirits

choices.text: Name every false omen you gave, and the land that paid for it

effects.log: You name them, if there are any, and the villages that learned to spit at a painted bird, and the years the tyrants kept because of you. The Qilin listens with its head low. "Knowing is the half of it," it says. The tortoise writes for a long time, or for no time at all.

choices.text: Say there were none

effects.log: The tortoise checks the record. The serpent checks the tortoise. If it was true, the tortoise says so, and the Qilin bows. If it was not, the serpent says nothing at all, very loudly, and the Qilin looks at you with great sadness and asks the next question anyway.

choices.text: Ask whether a false omen given in good faith is still false

effects.log: "Yes," says the Qilin at once. Then, more slowly: "But the bird that gave it is not." The Yellow Dragon, which was asleep, says "Good," without opening its eyes.

events.text: The Qilin's second question: "And the ones you missed?" At the edge of the terrace, thin as the steam off a rice pot, stand old scholars and old kings, the worthy who died without ever seeing you. One of them is saying, very quietly, the words every one of them said at the end: the phoenix does not come; I am finished.
events.arc: The Court of the Four Spirits

choices.text: Go to them one by one, and let each of them see you now

effects.log: It takes a year. To each of them you come down in the measured dance, late, centuries late, on a terrace in the sky. Some of them weep. One of them, an old exile, says only, "There you are," and fades contentedly, like a lamp at dawn. (-6 health)

choices.text: Tell the Qilin that a phoenix cannot be everywhere

effects.log: "No," says the Qilin. "Nor can a qilin. That is why there are four of us, and why, even so, there are always these." It looks at the steam-thin crowd. "Remember them. That is all they ask."

choices.text: Ask whether you can still go to their graves

effects.log: "Graves are for the living," says the tortoise. "Go anyway," says the serpent. Over the next century, one by one, you sit on a branch above each grave at sunrise, and nobody below knows why the old trees in the scholars' cemeteries fill with birds.

events.text: The Qilin's third question is not for you. It turns to your mate, who has stood a little behind you all through the hearing, and asks: "You have flown beside this bird for a thousand years. When it was wrong, did it listen? When you were wrong, did it say so?" Your mate looks at you for a long time before answering.
events.arc: The Court of the Four Spirits

choices.text: Let them answer, and do not interrupt

effects.log: Your mate tells the court everything: the quarrel over the governor, the lean winters, the time you overruled them and were right, and the time you were not. It takes a day. You do not interrupt once. At the end the Qilin says, "That is what a pair is for," and the tortoise writes the whole of it down.

choices.text: Answer first, for both of you

effects.log: You answer before they can, well and at length. The Qilin waits until you are finished, and then turns back to your mate and asks again. Your mate's answer is shorter than yours, and kinder, and the court notices both.

choices.text: Sing the answer together, as a duet

ok.log: The song goes wrong in the middle and right at the end, as your songs do. The Qilin laughs, a sound like spring water. "The middle is the answer," it says.

fail.log: You both start on the same note and then each wait for the other, and the duet becomes a silence, and the silence goes on, and the Qilin, surprisingly, takes that as an answer too.

events.text: The Qilin's third question is for your mate, and your mate is not there. It stands a long moment looking at the empty place beside you, as if it can see the shape that used to fill it. "Who speaks for the other half of your name?" it asks.
events.arc: The Court of the Four Spirits

choices.text: Sing their half of the song, as you have every dawn since

effects.log: You sing it, both halves, on the terrace in the sky. The blue storm at the edge stops moving. The white frost lies down. When you finish, the Qilin bows its head to the empty place, not to you, and the tortoise writes a whole column in a hand nobody has seen it use before.

choices.text: Say that nobody can, and that you will not pretend to

effects.log: "Good," says the Qilin. "The ones who pretend are the ones who break." It stays beside the empty place for the rest of the hearing, so that it is not empty.

events.text: A witness is called: {npc}, a human of the upper heavens, in robes of white cloud, who bows to you as if you had met. "In a life long ago," {npc} tells the court, "I was paid to hold a net on a ridge for a hill-king, because two phoenixes nested on the mountain. On the third dawn one of them was in my net. I want the court to know what the bird did when I came to it with a knife."
events.arc: The Court of the Four Spirits

choices.text: Let {him} tell it

mem.note: bore witness for the Phoenix before the Four Spirits

effects.log: "It did nothing," {npc} says. "It looked at me. It did not struggle and it did not beg. It waited to see what kind of person I was. I have spent four lives trying to be the kind I was that morning." The tortoise writes it down. The serpent, for once, says nothing.

choices.text: Ask {him} which way {he} used the knife

effects.log: {npc} smiles. "On the net," {he} says. "And then on every other net on the ridge, all night, until the lord's men came. They were not pleased." The Qilin, for the first time in the hearing, laughs.

events.text: A witness is called: {npc}, a human of the upper heavens, who once, in a life below, stood in a palace courtyard while a court played the ancient music in nine movements, and saw two birds come down at the ninth, and turn, and ask {him} whether they should stay. "The king had a crime under the throne," {npc} says. "I want the court to know that the birds asked a human, and listened to the answer."
events.arc: The Court of the Four Spirits

choices.text: Let {him} tell it

mem.note: bore witness at the Court of the Four Spirits

effects.log: {npc} tells it plainly: the music, the measured dance, the question, the answer. "I was afraid," {he} says, "and they waited until I was not." The Yellow Dragon opens both eyes for this, and keeps them open.

choices.text: Ask {him} whether {he} answered rightly

effects.log: {npc} thinks about it in front of the Four Spirits for a long time. "I do not know," {he} says at last. "But it was mine to answer, and they let it be mine." The serpent nods, as if that were the only thing that mattered.

events.text: The Qilin stops in front of you and looks at a dull place on your body, where a pattern once shone and went out like brass in the rain. "You came for a worthy reign," it says, "and you stayed when it was no longer worthy. Why?"
events.arc: The Court of the Four Spirits

choices.text: "I loved them"

effects.log: "Yes," says the Qilin gently. "That is always why. And you cannot sit here loving a reign more than the people under it." It does not send you away. It tells you where a worthy reign of that virtue is rising, and waits.

choices.text: "I hoped it would recover"

effects.log: "Hope is a good reason to watch," says the Qilin. "It is a poor reason to be seen." The tortoise writes it on the shell, and the serpent underlines it, which the serpent does not often do.

choices.text: "I did not notice in time"

effects.log: The Qilin is quiet a while. "Then taste the springs more often," it says. "Iron comes into the water years before it comes into the law."

events.text: The hearing stops. The Qilin has turned its head toward the world below, the way a deer turns at a sound, and the whole court turns with it. Far down, in a land you once came in the dance for, the palace spring tastes of iron, and you are still there, in the people's eyes, blessing it. "Go and leave it," says the Qilin, not unkindly. "Then come back. We will wait."
events.arc: The Court of the Four Spirits

choices.text: Go down and leave the land at once

effects.log: You fly down the light. (Leave the Land: the Qilin will not seat a bird whose blessing still hangs over a rotting reign.)

choices.text: Argue that the reign may still recover

ok.log: The Qilin listens. "Perhaps," it says. "Then go and watch it recover. From somewhere else." (Leave the Land.)

fail.log: The Qilin does not argue. It only goes on looking down at the land below, with its single soft horn, until you look too, and see the full prisons. (Leave the Land.)

events.text: The Vermilion Bird comes up from the south in a column of heat, every feather a flame, voice like a temple bell rung by a child, and lands on the edge of the Four Spirits' terrace, which is not its terrace. It does not read your record. It sings it. Every reign, every dance, every leaving. It sings very well. At the false omens, if there are any, its voice goes low and hot.
events.arc: The Court of the Four Spirits

choices.text: Listen to the end, and do not flinch

effects.log: When it ends, the Bird looks at you a long time, then, unexpectedly, bows. "You are not fire," it says. "I keep forgetting. You listened anyway."

choices.text: Sing the last verse with it

ok.log: Fire and wood, one verse. The Bird laughs so hard it sets fire to the Tortoise's record, and the serpent has to put it out, and the court is adjourned for a day.

fail.log: Your voice and its voice meet in the air and the air catches. Your tail is singed at the tip for a decade. The Bird is very sorry, and also laughing. (-8 health)

events.text: You take your place on the terrace, and for the first time the Four Spirits are four: the Qilin, which asks; the Tortoise, which records; the Yellow Dragon, which listens; and you, which comes. The Qilin walks to the middle of the circle, where nothing bends under its feet, and says: "The record is read. Now tell us when you will come."
events.arc: The Court of the Four Spirits

choices.text: "When a reign is worthy, and not before"

effects.log: "Then come," says the Qilin, as if that settles everything, and it does. The tortoise writes it on the shell. The serpent nods once. The Yellow Dragon lets out a breath like wind over ripe barley.

choices.text: "When the people need to see me, worthy reign or not"

effects.log: The Qilin is silent so long that the stars move. "That is not the old rule," it says at last. "It may be a better one. Be careful with it." The Yellow Dragon opens one eye and keeps it on you for a century.

choices.text: "I do not know yet. I will learn it from the paulownias"

effects.log: "Good," says the Yellow Dragon, which was not asleep. "The ones who know already are the ones we have to replace." The court does not end. It simply begins, and you are part of it.

choices.text: "When I am called by music that is true"

effects.log: "True music is rare," says the Qilin. "Good. So should you be." Far below, in nine courts at once, a music master wakes in the night certain the pipes are out of tune.

events.text: The Qilin comes to you alone at the edge of the terrace one evening, after many years of sittings, and stands beside you looking down at the lands under heaven. "You could stay," it says. "Here, for good, in this seat. Whenever a land is at peace, someone in it would see two birds at sunrise. Or you could go on. There is a further shape for a phoenix, past this one. Very few have taken it. I do not know what it costs."
events.arc: The Court of the Four Spirits

choices.text: Stay, and take the seat for good

effects.log: You stay. The terrace takes your weight the way a branch takes it. From now on, whenever a land under heaven is at peace, someone in it looks up at sunrise and sees two birds, and does not know why they are weeping.

choices.text: Go on toward the further shape

effects.log: "Then go," says the Qilin, "and come back and tell me." It walks away over the cloud without bending it. You understand that you will not come back the same thing, and that it knows.

choices.text: Ask for another century to decide

effects.log: "A century is short," says the tortoise. "For a bird it is long," says the serpent. The Qilin says nothing, and stands beside you, and the century begins.

events.text: The Vermilion Bird comes north in a column of heat and lands on the ridge opposite yours, and every paulownia between you curls its leaves. It is the guardian of the south, of summer and fire, and it has been watching you for a thousand years with the eye of somebody who thinks you are a cousin who married badly. "The south wall of the sky is too big for one bird," it sings. "Share it with me. Fire and wood. They would paint us together."

choices.text: Tell it, kindly, that you are not a guardian

effects.log: "I hold nothing," you say. "I only come." The Bird looks at you for a long time out of an eye like a coal. "That," it says, "is the most frightening thing I have ever heard a bird say." It does not leave.

choices.text: Ask what it would want from you in return

effects.log: "Company," it says, surprisingly. "The guardians hold their walls alone. Every summer I burn, and every summer nobody burns with me." Then, quickly: "Not that I mind."

choices.text: Say that if it wants the south, it can have all of it

effects.log: "I have all of it," says the Bird, offended, and then, after a while, laughs, a shower of sparks that sets three paulownias smouldering. "I came to share, not to be given. You do not understand fire at all."

events.text: The Vermilion Bird is back, and it has brought the south with it: a summer that will not end. The paulownias on your slope are going brown at the edges in the ninth month. "Then fight me for it," it sings. "If you will not share the south, take it. Guardians are made that way."

choices.text: Fly off the duel. You do not strike first

effects.log: You rise and fly north, out of the heat, and do not look back. The Bird follows you for a hundred li, singing insults, and then stops, and the summer ends that night, all at once, like a door closing.

choices.text: Sing it the five notes until it cools

ok.log: Wood answers fire with music, not with more fire. The Bird listens to the end with its flames low and blue. "Cousin," it says, which it has never said, and goes home south with the summer folded under its wing.

fail.log: It sings over you, and the summer stays a month too long, and one of your trees, the old one by the spring, cracks in the heat. (-12 health)

choices.text: Ask your mate to sing with you, both voices against the fire

effects.log: Two voices against one fire. The Bird is outnumbered, and knows it, and laughs. "Pairs," it says, with enormous scorn, and with something that is not scorn at all. It goes south. The paulownias put out new leaves in the tenth month.

events.text: A last visit. The Vermilion Bird lands on your branch, small and almost cool, the way it is only in the dead of winter. "They paint us together," it says. "Every painter in the south. Every banner. Red bird, five-coloured bird, nobody can tell which is which. I used to mind. Do you?"

choices.text: "No. Let them paint us together"

effects.log: The Bird is quiet a while. "Good," it says at last, and leans against you very slightly, which singes nothing at all. From then on the southern painters, without knowing why, always leave a little space between the two birds.

choices.text: "Yes. I am not fire, and you are not a pair"

effects.log: "True," says the Bird, without offence. "Then they can be wrong about both of us." It flies south, and you part as cousins, which is what you were.

choices.text: Give it a feather, so the painters have one thing right

effects.log: One five-coloured feather. The Bird holds it a long time without burning it, which costs it something. It is never seen in the south again without it.

events.text: Drums in the capital, and a new word in them. The ruler below is no longer a king. The ruler is an emperor, by proclamation, because the old empire across the river has grown weak and a vassal does not need its permission any more. Heralds read out what this means. Yellow robes. A new name for the years. And, in the third paragraph, the throne halls: a king sits under phoenixes; an emperor sits under dragons.

choices.text: Fly to the main throne hall and watch them begin

effects.log: The painters build scaffolds to the ceiling and begin to scrape. Gold flakes come down like snow on the empty throne. The two carved birds that have faced each other in clouds above that throne for three hundred years come down in pieces, and the painters do not look at them as they do it.

choices.text: Ask the court why a dragon is worth more than a pair of birds

effects.log: The ministers explain it very carefully. Dragons are an emperor's. Phoenixes are a king's. It is not about worth; it is about rank. They seem relieved when you leave. Nobody has ever explained rank to the Phoenix before.

choices.text: Take no notice. Ceilings are for humans

effects.log: You fly to your paulownia and let them scrape. All the same, the next morning you find yourself on the roof ridge of the throne hall, listening to the scrapers, and you are not sure how you got there.

events.text: The new ceilings go up. In the throne halls of three palaces two yellow dragons coil among the clouds above the emperor's seat, yellow for the centre, and the canopy over the throne has dragons too. They are very good dragons. The painters are proud of them. One of the painters, an old man, has kept a scrap of the gold he scraped off your old ceiling in a twist of paper, and he does not know why.

choices.text: Land on the old painter's windowsill and look at the scrap

effects.log: He sees you. He opens the paper and holds the scrap of gold out on his palm, as if returning something. You look at it a long time and do not take it. He keeps it all his life, and his granddaughter keeps it after him.

choices.text: Go and look at the dragons, fairly

effects.log: You sit on a beam in the half-dark under the new ceiling and look at the dragons for a whole day. They are good. They are not you. Nobody was ever going to confuse them, and you find that you are glad.

choices.text: Tell your mate it does not matter, and see if they believe you

effects.log: "It does not matter," you say. "No," your mate agrees, and you sit together on the roof of the scraped hall all night, not minding.

events.text: There is one hall they forgot. It is the old audience hall of the eastern palace, which the new emperor never uses: it is too far from the gate and the floor is cold. Nobody sent painters. Under its dusty ceiling, about as high above the throne as fifteen men standing on each other's shoulders, two carved phoenixes still face each other among clouds, gold and red and green, and look down on an empty seat.

choices.text: Go in and sit on the beam beside them

effects.log: It is very quiet. The wood birds have your crest and a second bird's long tail, more or less. The carver could only ever see one of you at a time, and it shows. You sit with them until dusk and feel, absurdly, that you are visiting relatives.

choices.text: Keep the hall forgotten: drive off any minister who wants to repaint it

effects.log: Twice in a few years a minister comes to measure the ceiling for dragons. Twice a five-coloured bird is waiting on the beam, looking down at him. The second minister writes in his report that the hall is unsuitable, and does not say why.

choices.text: Leave it be. It does not need you to be what it is

effects.log: You leave it. Years later, flying over, you see the hall's door open and children playing on the cold floor under the carved birds, and that seems right.

events.text: The empire does not last. Nothing that proclaims itself in a hurry does. The dragon halls are closed, then sold off as offices, then shut up with planks across the doors. The old forgotten hall, the cold one with the carved phoenixes, is the only throne hall in the city that still looks like a throne hall, because nobody ever bothered to change it. People have started coming to stand under its ceiling and look up.

choices.text: Watch them look up

effects.log: Old people, young people, a scholar with a sketchbook, a child on a parent's shoulders. They look up at the two wooden birds in the clouds for a long time, and some of them bow, to nobody, to a ceiling. You watch them from the roof ridge and do not come down.

choices.text: Come down and sit on the empty throne for a moment

effects.log: One morning, before the first visitors, you land on the throne. It is cold and much too big. You sit there a moment under the two carved birds and then fly out through the high window, and the guard who saw it tells nobody, all his life, except his children.

events.text: One night you find that you are tired of flying. Not of living: of flying. You are sitting on the beam beside the two carved birds in the cold forgotten hall, and the wood under your feet is warm, and you notice that there is room, exactly, between the two carvings, for a phoenix and a phoenix to face each other among the clouds and watch every ruler who ever sits below, for five hundred years.

choices.text: Not yet. There are living paulownias

effects.log: You stay on the beam until dawn, then fly out to the slope where the paulownias are. The room between the carvings will keep. Wood is patient.

choices.text: Go into the wood

effects.log: You go into the carved cloud the way a bird goes into a hollow, and your mate comes after you, or the memory of your mate, and the wood closes. For five hundred years you watch every ruler who sits on that cold seat, and some of them look up, and some of them do not dare.

events.text: A new state is being made below: not a kingdom, its makers insist, but something meant to outlast kings, with councils and offices and a seal for whoever holds the highest of them. The seal-cutter has been told to put a beast on it. Ministers have argued for a year. A dragon, a tiger, a pair of birds. The seal-cutter, {npc}, has climbed to your slope with a block of pale jade and a candle to ask you to sit.
events.arc: The Two Birds and the Flower

choices.text: Sit for {him}, all night, by the candle

effects.log: {npc} draws you a hundred times and throws away ninety-nine. "There is always a second bird in the drawings," {he} says, puzzled, "and I only see one of you."

choices.text: Ask {him} why a new state wants an old omen

effects.log: "Because a new state has no old anything," says {npc}, "and the people are frightened of new things. Two birds have been over thrones since before their great-grandparents. They will trust a seal that looks like their grandparents' ceilings."

choices.text: Tell {him} to carve the dragon. You are not for seals

effects.log: {npc} nods slowly, and goes down the mountain, and for a year the ministers argue on, and in the end, {npc} writes to you, they chose the dragon for the knob of the great seal. For the face, they still have not decided.

events.text: {npc} comes back with a design. Two birds facing each other with their long tails curving down, and between them a flower: the hibiscus that grows in every village hedge, that blooms a new flower every morning all summer and never seems to stop. "The office will change hands every few years," {he} says. "The flower is for that. The two birds are for whoever holds it to be measured against."
events.arc: The Two Birds and the Flower

choices.text: Look at the design for a long time, then sing one note: yes

effects.log: {npc} cuts it that winter. Two birds, a flower, the jade warm under {his} hands. When it is done {he} presses it once on red paper and brings the print up the mountain to show you, and it is the first time you have ever seen what you look like to humans, facing its other half.

choices.text: Ask {him} what happens when an unworthy hand holds it

effects.log: "Then the birds watch an unworthy hand," says {npc}. "And everybody who sees the seal sees them watching. I cannot make the office worthy. I can make it ashamed."

choices.text: Ask {him} to carve the birds a little apart, not touching

effects.log: {npc} carves them a hair apart, so a line of light goes between them in every print. "Room," {he} says, understanding. "Even a pair needs room." The ministers never notice. Anyone who has shared a nest does.

events.text: The seal has outlived three holders of the office already. One was good. One was ordinary. One, the third, pressed it on orders that filled the prisons, and in the villages people say that on those papers the two birds looked away from each other. Some say they have seen it. Nobody can prove it either way.
events.arc: The Two Birds and the Flower

choices.text: Fly over the capital the day the third holder leaves office

effects.log: You do not come down. You only pass overhead at noon, high, and keep going. The crowd at the gate sees you and goes quiet, and then someone begins, very softly, to laugh.

choices.text: Let the story be. People need the birds to look away sometimes

effects.log: You let it be. A rumour that the birds on the seal can refuse a bad order is, you decide, more use to the people below than anything you could do about it.

events.text: The seal-cutter's descendant climbs your slope with the old jade in a silk bag. {npc} cuts seals too, and has been told what every child of the family is told: that the two birds on the great seal were drawn from a real one, on this slope, by candlelight. "The family says you can put yourself into the stone," {npc} says. "If you want. Not your body. What you are. So the seal is not only a picture."
events.arc: The Two Birds and the Flower

choices.text: Tell {him} a seal should be only a picture

effects.log: {npc} nods, and puts the jade back in the silk bag, a little relieved. "The family always said you would say that," {he} admits. "They said that was why you were chosen."

choices.text: Go into the seal

effects.log: You put what you are into the two birds and the flower, and {npc} presses the seal once on red paper and weeps without knowing why. For as long as the office lasts, whoever holds it feels two birds watching every paper they seal, and every one of them, worthy or not, is measured.

events.text: In the south, a small kingdom of rivers and fine craft is in its last years. Its temple workshop cast, long ago, a great incense burner: a dragon for a base, a lid of mountain peaks with tigers and immortals and five musicians on it, and on the very top a bird with its wings spread, which the casters swore was drawn from life. When the monks burn incense in it the smoke comes out of the mountains. The bird is you, or near enough. Armies are coming up the river.

choices.text: Go and look at the bronze bird

effects.log: It is good. Better than good: the caster saw how your neck goes when you are about to sing. The five little musicians below play a flute, a zither, a drum, a pipe and a lute, and the incense comes up between the peaks round them like weather.

choices.text: Sing over the kingdom one last time

effects.log: You sing over the river capital at dusk. In the temple workshop, the monks stop work and listen. The kingdom has a few years left. It spends them, the chroniclers say afterwards, unusually well.

choices.text: Stay away. A falling kingdom is not yours to bless

effects.log: You stay away. But on the road north you pass the army coming up the river, and it is very large, and you find you are flying slowly.

events.text: The night the capital falls, the workshop monks do not run. They drag the great burner out of the hall to the workshop by the smoke vent, where there is a wooden trough of water for quenching, and they lower it in, carefully, the way one lays a sick person into a bath, and heap roof tiles and broken jars over the trough. Above them on the beam, in the dark, you are watching.

choices.text: Stay on the beam until they have finished, and keep watch for them

effects.log: Soldiers pass the workshop twice and do not come in. Something on the beam above the door makes their torches gutter. By dawn the monks are gone, and the trough is only a pile of rubbish, and the river kingdom is over.

choices.text: Come down and let the monks see you, so they know

effects.log: The oldest monk sees you in the lamplight and stops with a roof tile in his hands. He looks from you to the bronze bird under the water and back. Then he bows, and goes on burying it, faster and steadier.

events.text: Decades, then centuries. The workshop rots, the temple burns, the trough fills with silt, and rice fields are planted over the place, and then a yard for the oxcarts of a market, and then rice again. Every few decades you fly over and feel it under the mud, the bronze bird, wings spread, in the dark: a phoenix that nobody remembers is there.

choices.text: Land in the paddy above it and stand there a while

effects.log: A farmer sees a five-coloured bird standing in the shallow water of his paddy in the morning, absolutely still, looking down. He tells his family. His family tell him he was dreaming. He plants that corner of the field last every year, for the rest of his life, and does not know why.

choices.text: Let it be forgotten. Forgetting is safe

effects.log: You let it be. Forgotten things are not melted down for arrowheads. You know that from the crowns.

events.text: One autumn, flying over the old river kingdom, you feel the bronze bird under the mud call to you, the way the high ridge once called to your mate. It is lonely down there, and it has been lonely for a long time, and it has your shape. There is room in it.

choices.text: Sing to it from above, and fly on

effects.log: You sing it the five notes from the sky, so it knows it is remembered, and fly on. Under the mud, if bronze can listen, it listens.

choices.text: Go down into the mud with it

effects.log: You go down into the dark and into the bronze, wings spread above five musicians who never stop playing. Fourteen hundred years later a digger's spade strikes something in the mud of a workshop trough, and the first thing that comes up into the light is a bird.

events.text: A court you once came in the dance for, one that did not deserve it, has been using you ever since. Your picture is on its banners. Its heralds read your coming at every proclamation. Now the chamberlain has sent a cage up the mountain: gilded, as tall as three men, with a perch of sandalwood and a dish of the best millet in the land. "For the coronation," says the note. "Heaven's favour should be seen."

choices.text: Break the cage on the rocks

effects.log: It takes you all night. Gilt comes off on your feathers. By morning the cage is kindling and the bearers have run, and the chamberlain writes in the record that the Phoenix was too modest to accept so great an honour.

choices.text: Fly over the coronation, high, and keep going

effects.log: Everyone in the square sees you pass over, high, and not stop, and not look down. Nobody says anything. The heralds read the proclamation of heaven's favour anyway, to a very quiet crowd.

choices.text: Ignore it. It is only a cage

effects.log: You ignore it. The cage stands at the foot of the mountain all winter, empty, with the millet in the dish going grey, and the people who pass it begin to call it the Phoenix's house, and do not mean it kindly.

events.text: In the villages under the false reign, people have learned to spit when they see two birds on a banner. A child throws a stone at a painted phoenix on a gate. Her mother does not stop her. You see it from the roof.

choices.text: Fly down to the gate and let the child see the real one

effects.log: The child looks at you, and at the painted bird, and at you. "Then why did you come for him?" she asks. You have no answer for her, and you let her see that you have none.

choices.text: Go and drink at the cleanest spring you know, and stay away a season

effects.log: A season away, at a spring under a pine. It does not mend anything in the village. It mends a little of you, which is the part you can reach.

choices.text: Leave the land, in sight of everyone

effects.log: You go up to the palace roof at noon. (Leave the Land: the people will read it.)

events.text: The cage comes again, under a new chamberlain who has read the old records. This time there is a sweet spring in it: water carried up from a temple courtyard in sealed jars, poured into a stone basin inside the bars. It smells of rice wine and clean rock. Your throat aches at it. The door is open.

choices.text: Turn away from the water

effects.log: You turn away from the stolen spring with your throat aching and fly a hundred li to a ditch-dry valley where there is no water at all, and it is better. (-8 health)

choices.text: Smash the basin so no other bird is tempted

effects.log: The stone basin cracks and the water runs out between the bars into the dust. The new chamberlain looks at the wet dust a long time, and goes back down the mountain with a very different report.

choices.text: Bow, and let the door close behind you

effects.log: You bow. The door closes softly, the way doors in palaces do. Every coronation for two hundred years, they carry the cage out before the gate, and the people learn to curse two birds on a banner, and you learn to sit very still on the sandalwood perch and look at nobody.

events.text: The false reign has fallen, as false reigns do. In the ransacked palace, the gilded cage lies on its side in a courtyard with the door hanging open. Children are playing in it. One of them is sitting on the sandalwood perch, flapping their arms, squawking: they are playing at the coronation bird.

choices.text: Watch from the wall until they get bored and go home

effects.log: They play coronation for an hour, then soldiers, then ghosts, then go home for dinner. Nobody plays the coronation bird again after that summer. You decide that is the best thing that could have happened to it.

choices.text: Land on top of the cage

effects.log: The children freeze. Then the one on the perch, very slowly, climbs out of the open door and bows to you, and runs. In the village they say the real Phoenix came to see the cage empty, and laughed. You did not laugh. But you see why they say so.

events.text: The store is empty, and the groves are bare, and it is the first month. A sparrow lands on the branch beside you, looks you over for some time, and says: "You are as thin as we are in a bad winter. The market at the crossroads spills millet every day at noon. We go at noon. You might as well come."

choices.text: Go to the market at noon

effects.log: You go. You do not peck, quite. You stand on a stall roof in the noise and the dust with the sparrows and look down at the spilled millet for an hour, and a peddler in a horsehair hat looks up at you for an hour, thinking.

choices.text: Fly instead to the farthest sweet spring you know

effects.log: Three days of flying, hungry, to a spring under a pine on a hill nobody climbs. You drink. The sparrow does not follow. Behind you, at the crossroads, the market spills its millet at noon for somebody else. (-6 health)

choices.text: Thank the sparrow, and fast

effects.log: "Suit yourself," says the sparrow, not unkindly, and goes. A phoenix may fly a thousand li hungry. You remember that, in the cold, and it helps. (-10 health)

events.text: The peddler in the horsehair hat is in the market again. He has spent a week asking a poultry seller, again and again, whether the dull long-tailed bird on the stall roof is a phoenix, until the poultry seller, worn down, says yes, it is a phoenix, and the peddler offers to buy it at ten times the price of a cock. He is looking up at you with a sack in his hands.

choices.text: Fly away, now, before the sack

ok.log: You are off the roof before the sack comes up. Behind you the peddler shrugs and buys the poultry seller's biggest cock instead, and you hear him calling it a phoenix all the way to the magistrate's gate.

fail.log: The sack comes down on you. You tear out of it on the second try and leave a tail feather in the peddler's hand. He sells the feather that afternoon, as a phoenix's, and is, for once, telling the truth. (-10 health)

choices.text: Sing, once, from the roof, the five notes

ok.log: The whole market stops. The poultry seller drops a hen. The peddler takes off his horsehair hat, slowly, and holds it against his chest. Nobody buys you. You fly to the hills and do not come back to the crossroads.

fail.log: Your voice cracks on the third note, and the market laughs, and the peddler laughs loudest. "A phoenix," he says, "with a cold." You fly off with your face burning, if a bird has a face.

choices.text: Stay on the roof and let him try

effects.log: He takes you to the magistrate in the sack as a phoenix. The magistrate looks at a dull, dusty, millet-fed bird and has the peddler beaten for selling a chicken, and the peddler laughs all the way home, because the poultry seller paid him back twice. You are kept in the yard with the hens. In time, you forget.

events.text: Years after the crossroads market, the peddler's grandchild sells pictures of a phoenix in the same square: a dull long-tailed bird on a stall roof, very funny, the story of how grandfather sold a chicken to a magistrate. Everybody buys one. Nobody knows that the bird in the picture was real, except the bird.

choices.text: Buy nothing, and laugh, if a phoenix can

effects.log: You sit on the same stall roof, clean now, five-coloured, and look down at a hundred funny pictures of yourself at your worst. The grandchild looks up and does not recognise you at all, and that, somehow, is the funniest part.

choices.text: Leave a true feather on the grandchild's stall

effects.log: The grandchild finds a long five-coloured feather on the stall in the morning, and stops selling the funny pictures, and starts to paint a different one, which nobody buys, and which is very good.

events.text: Year after year you have stayed in a land you once blessed, while it rotted under you. You told yourself you were loyal. Now a geomancer from the north is at the king's ear, a soft-voiced stranger nobody can quite remember hiring. "The capital is a phoenix's nest," he tells the king. "That is why the bird has stayed. Make it eggs, and it will never leave, and your line will never end."

choices.text: Leave now, before the eggs are built

effects.log: You rise from the palace roof at noon, late, years late, but in full sight. (Leave the Land: it is still not too late to go.)

choices.text: Stay and watch what the stranger does

effects.log: The king believes him. Of course the king believes him: he is telling the king that the bird will never leave. By spring the whole city is out with baskets, heaping earth.

choices.text: Go to the geomancer at night and ask him who sent him

effects.log: He is not afraid of you. "Somebody who wants this kingdom to be finished," he says, rolling up a map. "Like you do, if you are honest. You only cannot bring yourself to finish it."

events.text: The earth eggs rise all over the capital: round mounds as high as houses, grassed over, a dozen, then twenty. The people heap them in the evenings after work. They are proud of them. They bring their children to stand on top. "So the Phoenix never leaves," they say, and wave up at you on the palace roof.

choices.text: Stand on the highest egg, so they see you are still here

effects.log: They cheer. You have never been cheered by so many people at once, and it is for staying in a rotten place. It warms you anyway. That is the worst part.

choices.text: Fly from egg to egg at night, trying to understand the shape of the land

ok.log: From high enough, at night, with the lamps lit, you see it: the plain is not a nest. It is long, and narrow at both ends, with the river along one side like a keel. It is a boat. The eggs are cargo. The more they heap, the lower it sits.

fail.log: You fly over them for a month and see only mounds, and lamps, and proud people asleep, and the river that has been rising a little, every year, for as long as you have watched.

events.text: The geomancer is leaving. You see him go at dawn, alone, with a spade, through the chestnut grove at the edge of the capital. In the grove he stops, and digs, all morning, very fast: a well, straight down, into the wet. Then he throws the spade in the well, and runs north. Behind him, slowly, the water in the well begins to rise.

choices.text: Go after him

effects.log: You catch him at the river. He looks up at you and laughs, quite kindly. "A hole in the bottom of the boat," he says. "I did not sink it. It was sinking. I only made it honest." You let him go. You cannot think of a reason not to.

choices.text: Go to the king and tell him what the land is

effects.log: The king listens to you, and then to his ministers, who tell him that the Phoenix has been under a great strain, and that the eggs are working: look, the bird is still here. The king chooses the ministers. You knew he would.

choices.text: Stand in the chestnut grove and look down into the well

effects.log: The water is very clear. At the bottom, far down, you can see your own reflection, five-coloured, alone. You stand there until noon.

events.text: The kingdom is going down, and everyone can feel it: not a flood, not a war, only a long slow tilt, like a boat taking water. Ministers flee north with their families. The earth eggs stand in the empty streets. On the palace roof, where you have sat all these years, the tiles are cold and nobody looks up any more.

choices.text: Leave, at last, in sight of the last people in the streets

effects.log: You rise from the roof. The last people in the streets look up and see the bird leave the nest at last, and they understand, and so do you, and you fly north through the rain without looking back. (Leave the Land.)

choices.text: Fly the last families out to the hills ahead of the water

effects.log: You fly ahead of a column of carts all the way to high ground, singing so they can follow you through the rain. Then you go back for the next column. It takes the whole winter. When it is over the kingdom is gone, and you are not in it. (-10 health)

choices.text: Stay. You blessed it. You will go down with it

effects.log: You stay. The land goes down, slow, the way the old say a ship goes down, a little at a time and then all at once. The eggs were cargo. You sink with them, on the palace roof, facing south, singing nobody's half of the song.

events.text: A hill-king in the north-east is to be buried, and his crown is not finished. The crown-makers want five colours on it: a gilt-bronze band, uprights like branching trees, and between them real bird feathers, blue, white, red, black, yellow, the colours of heaven's own bird. They have hired the best feather-takers in three kingdoms. Their nets are already on your ridge.

choices.text: Move your roost to a farther mountain

effects.log: A hard move, in the wrong season. You grumble about the sticks for a year. But the nets on the old ridge catch only wind, and a crow, which the feather-takers let go with a curse.

choices.text: Go to the crown-makers' workshop and see what they want

effects.log: In the workshop a gilt-bronze band lies on the bench with empty sockets along its uprights: little tubes, each the width of a quill. Twenty of them. The crown-maker is an old woman, very skilled. She looks at you in the doorway, and at the sockets, and does not get up.

choices.text: Cut the nets in the night

ok.log: Every net on the ridge, by beak, by dawn. The feather-takers wake to strips of cord in the wind, and look at each other, and one of them says quietly that perhaps they should take the job in the south after all.

fail.log: The last net is a trap behind a trap. You tear out of it bleeding and with three tail feathers gone, and somewhere a crown-maker is pleased. (-12 health)

events.text: The feather-takers have set the oldest trap in their trade on your slope: a ring of polished bronze mirrors round a dish of the finest millet, so that a phoenix coming down to look will see a whole flock of phoenixes at the dish, and think it safe, and land. It is a good trap. It only works on a bird that has forgotten what it is.

choices.text: Look at yourself in the mirrors a long time, and fly away

effects.log: Twenty of you in the mirrors, five-coloured, all looking back. None of them would peck millet. You fly away, and the feather-takers, watching from the pines, curse very quietly.

choices.text: Smash the mirrors

effects.log: Bronze mirrors do not smash; they ring. You knock them flat one by one, and they ring all down the valley like temple bells, and every village for ten li knows what is happening on the Phoenix's slope.

choices.text: Land among the mirrors and eat the millet

effects.log: You land. You eat. The net comes down from the pines. Your five colours go into the sockets of a gilt-bronze crown, one feather to each, blue, white, red, black, yellow, and the crown goes into the hill-king's tomb with him, and the tomb is closed, and it is very dark, and you are very beautiful in it.

events.text: They have taken your mate. You come back to the paulownia at dusk and the nest is empty and there are cut cords on the branch and a smell of bronze. The crown-makers' workshop is three days north. The hill-king is to be buried at the full moon.

choices.text: Fly north and take them back, whatever it costs

ok.log: You come down on the workshop at midnight like a falling star. The feather-takers run. Your mate is in a wicker cage by the bench, alive, missing two wing feathers. You fly home together slowly, and the hill-king is buried with an empty crown. (-15 health)

fail.log: You come down on the workshop at midnight and the nets are waiting for you too. You tear free, barely. Your mate does not. You are on the roof when the cage goes out to the tomb, and you hear the old crown-maker weeping as she works. (-30 health)
fail.deathCause: the feather-takers' nets, at the crown-makers' workshop

choices.text: Go to the old crown-maker and plead for them

ok.log: The old crown-maker listens to a bird plead for a bird, in a voice like a zither, and puts down her tools. She opens the wicker cage herself. "The king can be buried with gold," she says. "Gold does not mind."

fail.log: She listens, and weeps, and does not open the cage. "My family will hang if the crown is bare," she says. You understand. You do not forgive. Your mate's colours go into the tomb at the full moon.

choices.text: Sing to your mate from the roof so they are not alone in the cage

effects.log: Every night until the full moon you sing from the workshop roof, and every night your mate answers from the cage, more quietly. On the last night they do not answer. The crown goes into the tomb at dawn, and the other half of your name is silent.

events.text: Centuries on, robbers open the hill-king's tomb, and then scholars open what the robbers left, and in the lamplight there is a gilt-bronze crown with empty sockets along its uprights, and in one of them the quill of a single five-coloured feather, still blue. The scholars handle it as if it were alive. Word comes to you on the wind.

choices.text: Fly to the hall where they keep it, and look through the window

effects.log: One blue quill in a gilt socket under glass-clear lamplight. A scholar is writing a long label for it. You sit on the windowsill until dusk, and the scholar looks up once, and stops writing for a long time.

choices.text: Let it be. It is a crown, not a bird

effects.log: You let it be. It is a crown now, and people are mourning the right thing at last, and that is not nothing.

events.text: Winter, and you are back at the paulownia where your mate last sat. The branch is bare, and there is still one long feather caught in the twigs at the end of it, theirs. You sit on your end of the branch. The other end is empty. At midnight the moon comes up and hangs on it, exactly where they would have been.
events.arc: The Moon on the Empty Branch

choices.text: Sit, and do not eat, and do not leave

effects.log: You sit there all winter. The moon comes every clear night and hangs on the empty end. You begin, against all sense, to wait for it. (-10 health)

choices.text: Sing their half of the song to the moon

effects.log: You sing their half. It comes out wrong. You sing it again. A woodcutter on the slope below stops with his load on his back and stands there in the snow until you are finished.

choices.text: Fly away from the tree at dawn, and not come back for a long time

effects.log: You go. Behind you the feather in the twigs lifts in the wind as if it were waving. You do not look.

events.text: An old scholar lives in a hut under the paulownia now, alone, and has noticed you. Every night {npc} comes out with a lamp and looks up at the bird on the near end of the branch and the moon on the far end, and goes back inside, and you hear a brush moving on paper. Tonight {he} reads aloud what {he} has written. It is three lines.
events.arc: The Moon on the Empty Branch

choices.text: Listen

mem.note: wrote three lines about the bird on the paulownia

effects.log: "I planted the paulownia to see the phoenix," {npc} reads. "It came, and the other did not. Only the bright moon hangs on the empty branch." Then {he} blows out the lamp and sits in the dark with you for a while. Every child will learn those lines. You do not know that yet.

choices.text: Fly down to the hut and sit on the lintel by {him}

effects.log: {npc} does not startle. {He} only shifts over on the step, as one does for a friend, and reads you the three lines, and then reads you everything else {he} ever wrote, most of it bad, all night.

events.text: Winter after winter on the branch. Your end is worn smooth. The feather in the twigs has gone grey. Tonight the moon comes up and hangs on the far end, as always, and for the first time you could swear it is waiting for you to move over.
events.arc: The Moon on the Empty Branch

choices.text: Make the vow: go on alone, for both

effects.log: You sing both halves, all the way through, without breaking, and at the end you make the vow: to go on, alone, for both. The moon slides off the far end of the branch and goes down behind the ridge, and you let it. (The Lone Vow.)

choices.text: Fly to the high ridge and sing until dawn, and decide nothing yet

effects.log: All night on the ridge. The mountains answer with two voices, as they always do. At dawn you go back to the branch. Not yet. Not tonight.

choices.text: Move over, onto the empty end, under the moon

effects.log: You move over. You sit where they sat. The moon is very close. You do not leave the branch again, and in the spring the village finds only one long feather on it, and a scholar's three lines nailed to the trunk, which every child will learn.

events.text: In a poor village in the hills a scholar who failed the state examinations four times keeps a one-room school, and sixty years ago planted a paulownia by the door to call the phoenix. You have known the tree for decades. You have never sat in it. Every dawn the scholar, {npc}, old now, comes out with a broom and sweeps the yard under it and looks up, and every dawn the branches are empty.

choices.text: Sit in the tree tomorrow at dawn

effects.log: You mean to. That night a reign three provinces away begins to rot, and you are needed there, and you go, and when you come back the yard under the paulownia is swept, and empty, and the scholar is older.

choices.text: Ask yourself why you never have

effects.log: Because the ruler of that land was never worthy, and you come only for the worthy. But the scholar is not a ruler. The thought is new, and it sits in you all summer like a seed.

choices.text: Keep away. The waiting is the scholar's life now

effects.log: You keep away. Below, every dawn, the broom, and the look up, and the empty branches, and the scholar going in to teach. The children have learned to look up too.

events.text: The old scholar has died in the winter. The village has buried the scholar on the slope above the school. The paulownia stands by the door, bare. The school is shut, because nobody else in the village can read well enough to teach, and the headman says the tree will be cut in spring for coffin boards and a wedding chest.

choices.text: Come, late, and sit in the tree in spring, and stay

effects.log: You come at the first green. The headman sees you from the yard and drops his axe. By evening the whole village is under the tree, and by the next spring a young scholar from the market town has asked to keep the school, because of the bird.

choices.text: Go to the scholar's grave first

effects.log: You sit on the grave marker at sunrise. Nobody sees. Then you fly down to the tree by the school door, and the headman sees that, and the axe stays in the shed.

events.text: The school by the paulownia has a teacher again, {npc}, young, poor, a little frightened of the children, and very frightened of you. Every dawn {he} sweeps the yard and looks up, and you are there, and {he} bows, and drops the broom.

choices.text: Sing the morning in, so the lesson starts on time

effects.log: Every dawn a song from the paulownia, and every dawn the teacher rings the bell on the last note. The village sets its day by it. The children are never late again, which the teacher considers the greatest miracle of the age.

choices.text: Drop a leaf on the hardest lesson of the day

effects.log: A heart-shaped leaf on the desk of whichever child is struggling. It becomes a custom: the leaf child gets help first. In a few years the village sends more scholars to the examinations than the market town.

events.text: Decades of springs in the paulownia by the school. Two teachers. Three generations of children. The tree has never been cut, and nobody alive remembers that anyone wanted to. One morning in spring you notice that you have not flown over a capital in a decade, and that you do not miss it.

choices.text: Not yet. There are reigns to watch

effects.log: You fly. The school bell rings on time without you; you taught it that. You come back every spring, and the children always know which morning, before the teacher does.

choices.text: Stay here for good

effects.log: You stay. The schoolhouse never lacks students, and the tree is never cut, and the dead scholar's grave on the slope above is the best-kept grave in the hills. Somewhere far off, rulers rise and fall without you, and the children of one poor village learn to read under a bird.

events.text: A small hill kingdom between the great ones, with a mountain fortress on its peak and old round tombs in its valley, sends its whole court up the mountain on foot. The king is young and has no army worth the name. He kneels on the bare rock below your paulownia. "My grandfather hung a hundred nets to keep you," he says. "I am taking them down. I am asking instead."

choices.text: Ask him what he would do with your staying

effects.log: "Nothing," says the young king. "That is the point. If you stay, my people will believe they are worth staying for. I would rather they believed that than anything I could tell them."

choices.text: Watch his court for three seasons before you answer

effects.log: Three seasons over his little capital: the granary open, the prison with two thieves in it, the music played badly by people who are not afraid. Not a great reign. A sound one.

choices.text: Fly over the ridge and look at the nets

effects.log: They are coming down. Old ones, rotten ones, a hundred of them, hauled off the ridge by the king's own household and burned in a heap at the foot of the mountain. The smoke goes straight up. Somebody has thought about how this would look to a bird.

events.text: The paulownias they have planted for you on the lower slopes are tall now: forty of them, in rows, a whole hillside of heart-shaped leaves. The children of the hill kingdom are named for the morning you first rose from the peak. Your mate has started to call the mountain home, out loud, which your mate has never said of any place.

choices.text: Agree with your mate: this is home

effects.log: "Home," you say. Your mate does not answer, only settles in the nest a little deeper, which is the answer.

choices.text: Remind your mate that a phoenix does not stay

effects.log: "I know," your mate says. "I only wanted to say it once." You both look down at the forty trees for a long time.

choices.text: Count the trees, and the names, and say nothing

effects.log: Forty trees. Eleven children named for a morning. One small king who took down a hundred nets. You count them all again in the spring, and the numbers have grown.

events.text: The young king is old. His heir is coming of age. The old king climbs the mountain one last time, very slowly, with a stick, and sits under your paulownia, and asks you nothing at all. He has brought rice cakes for himself and nothing for you, because he knows better.

choices.text: Sit with him until he goes down

effects.log: He eats his rice cakes and tells you about his grandchildren and goes down at dusk. He dies that winter. The heir climbs the mountain the next spring with the same stick, and asks you nothing, and that is how you know the kingdom will be all right.

choices.text: Come down to him, close, so he can see your patterns

effects.log: He looks at each pattern for a long time, head, wings, back, breast, belly. "So that is what it is," he says. "I always wondered." He goes down the mountain smiling, and is buried with his stick.

events.text: On the mountain they call the Flying Phoenix, after the morning you first rose from it, your mate sits beside you on the peak at dawn and says, very quietly, that they would like to stop flying away. Not to stop flying. Only to stop flying away. The kingdom below will keep its luck as long as you stay. You both know that it is not luck.

choices.text: Tell them gently: not yet. The rest of heaven is still waiting

effects.log: "Not yet," you say. Your mate is quiet a while. "But one day," they say. "One day," you agree, and the mountain hears it, and holds you to it.

choices.text: Stay on the mountain, the two of you, for good

effects.log: You stay. The kingdom below keeps its luck while you stay, and the mountain keeps its name, and every morning for the rest of your life two shadows cross its slope at sunrise, and the children below look up and count them, and argue.

events.text: The murim has a ranking for its young: the Rising Dragons and Phoenixes, the ten most promising fighters under thirty. Its compilers have climbed your mountain to ask if they may keep the name. "Some of the elders say it is presumptuous," says the eldest compiler. "To name children after heaven's bird. We thought we should ask the bird."

choices.text: Say yes, on one condition: the list must be honest

effects.log: "Honest," says the compiler, writing it down. "Not merely skilled. Honest." For three hundred years, every compiler of the list reads that line at their first meeting, and some of them even mean it.

choices.text: Ask why the dragon gets named first

effects.log: The compilers look at each other. "It sounds better," says one. "Phoenixes and Dragons," you try. It does not sound better. You let them keep the order. Somewhere far off, a coil of cloud seems pleased.

choices.text: Say the young should be named for themselves

effects.log: The compilers go down the mountain thoughtful. They keep the name anyway; by now it belongs to the murim. But the list, from that year, has a line for each fighter saying what they are named for, in their own words.

events.text: A young swordsman at the top of the Rising Dragons and Phoenixes, {npc}, has a great fight at dawn: a duel with the master of a rival school, the kind that ends one of them. {He} has climbed your mountain the night before, not to ask for anything, only to sit under your paulownia and not sleep.

choices.text: Fly over the duelling ground at dawn, so {he} sees two birds

mem.note: saw the Phoenix at dawn before the great fight

effects.log: {npc} looks up as you pass, and so does the old master, and both of them lower their swords a little. The duel happens. Nobody dies. Both schools swear afterwards that the bird came for their side.

choices.text: Sing {him} to sleep under the tree

mem.note: slept under the Phoenix's paulownia the night before a great fight

effects.log: {npc} sleeps three hours, which {he} says afterwards was the difference. {He} wins. {He} does not know whether to thank you, and climbs back up the mountain to ask, and you are not there.

choices.text: Ask {him} what {he} will do if {he} wins

effects.log: {npc} has not thought about it. {He} thinks about it all night. At dawn {he} goes down to the duel and, to everyone's astonishment, offers the rival master a draw. It is accepted. It is the most talked-about fight in a decade.

events.text: A grandmaster of ninety, {npc}, climbs your mountain with a cane. "I was never on the list," {he} says. "I was a slow learner. I am the best sword under heaven now, and I am ninety, and the list is for the young. I would like to be counted, once, among the Rising Dragons and Phoenixes. I thought I would ask the one who can."

choices.text: Count {him}: fly over {his} dawn practice tomorrow

mem.note: was counted among the Rising Dragons and Phoenixes at ninety

effects.log: {npc} is in the yard at dawn with a practice sword. You pass over, low. {He} lowers the sword and laughs until {he} has to sit down. The compilers, who hear about it, add a line to the bottom of the list that year: and one more, by the bird's own choice.

choices.text: Tell {him} the list was never for the young

effects.log: "It was for the promising," you say. "You have only just finished promising." {npc} looks at you a long time and then goes down the mountain without the cane, which {he} leaves under your tree.

choices.text: Duel {him}

ok.log: Wood against steel at dawn on the peak. You win without striking first, by the high branch and the morning sun and a voice from above. {npc} lies on the rock laughing. "Counted," {he} says. "Now I am counted."

fail.log: {npc} is very, very good. You fly off the duel at the last moment, with a cut on your wing, and {he} bows to the sky after you, delighted. (-12 health)

events.text: Decades of dawns over the fighting grounds, and the young who see two birds before their first great duel fight better, and more honestly, and more of them live. The list has become the murim's proudest thing. One morning, flying over a dawn practice yard, it comes to you that you could give yourself to this: not to the rulers, not to the heavens, but to the young, every generation, for good.

choices.text: Keep flying over the yards, as you are

effects.log: You keep flying over. The young keep looking up. It is enough, for now, to be the bird and not the name.

choices.text: Give yourself to the young

effects.log: You give yourself to it, and stop being a bird that comes, and become a name the young are given. In every generation after this one the most promising are called the Rising Dragons and Phoenixes, and the best of them, on the morning of their first great fight, look up and see two birds at dawn.

events.text: A thousand years of the two of you. You have counted it, roughly, by paulownias: planted, grown, cut for chests, planted again, over and over, in every village under heaven. This morning, on the high ridge, your mate sings the first half of the song and stops, and waits, and you realise that you no longer know which half was ever yours.

choices.text: Sing the other half, whichever it is

effects.log: You sing it. It is the right half. It was always going to be the right half. Below, in the paddies, an old farmer straightens up and tells his grandchild that this is what the old songs mean by harmony, and the grandchild does not believe him.

choices.text: Sing the same half, at the same time

effects.log: Both of you, the first half, at once, in unison, for the first time in a thousand years. It is very strange. It is almost funny. Your mate laughs in the middle of it, which no phoenix has done on a ridge in recorded history.

events.text: The land below is at peace. Not because of you: because a long line of ordinary rulers have been, one after another, a little better than the last, which is the only way it ever really happens. Your mate wants to go up the morning light again, all the way up, and this time not come down.

choices.text: Ask why now

effects.log: "Because nobody needs us," says your mate. "That is the best thing that has ever happened to us." You think about it all summer, and cannot find the flaw.

choices.text: Say that someone always needs you

effects.log: "Someone always will," your mate agrees. "That is why we have to choose a morning." They do not press you. They only start, every dawn, to fly a little higher before turning back.

events.text: The morning comes. Red sun over five-coloured cloud, the paulownias on the slope in full leaf, every reign below quiet. Your mate is on the high ridge already, wings half open, looking back at you, the way they looked back the first time you flew to the edge of heaven.

choices.text: One more spring

effects.log: "One more spring," you say. Your mate folds their wings and lands beside you. "There is always one more spring," they say, not unhappily. "That is the trouble with springs."

choices.text: Rise together on the morning sun, and do not come down

effects.log: You rise together on the morning sun, wing to wing, two shadows on the cloud and then none. You do not come down. That era is remembered as peace below, and nobody can say why, and the old songs about two birds flying together are sung at every wedding in the land for a thousand years.

events.text: Five patterns shine on you at once: virtue on the head, righteousness on the wings, propriety on the back, benevolence on the breast, trust on the belly. From the edge of heaven they can be read from a whole country away. Below, in a hundred villages, the shamans of the five directions have hung out their banners, blue, white, red, black and yellow, and turned to the morning sun to call for peace, and every one of them is looking at you.

choices.text: Go down to the nearest shaman's hill and stand under the banners

effects.log: The old shaman sees you land among the five banners, and stops the drum, and does not start it again. "Oh," she says. "It was you. All this time." The village does not finish the rite. There is no need.

choices.text: Stay at the edge of heaven and let them see you from afar

effects.log: You stay high. In a hundred villages the shamans finish the rite and look up and see, very far, five colours against the sunrise, and go home without saying anything, and sleep well.
