choices.text: Ask the Qilin what this is

effects.log: "The further shape," says the Qilin, walking beside you on the cloud without bending it. "You were a bird that came when there was peace. You are becoming the thing it comes from." It seems, for the first time since you met it, a little in awe.

events.text: Something is changing in you that has nothing to do with feathers. When you sleep in the paulownia, the land below sleeps better. When you wake, the springs taste a little sweeter in three provinces. You have stopped being a bird that appears in peace. You are starting to be where peace comes from, and you do not know if you like it.

choices.text: Lean into it

effects.log: You let it happen. You sleep, and the land sleeps. You sing, and in three provinces the courts are, for a year, unusually fair. It is very quiet work. Nobody thanks you, because nobody knows. That turns out to be the best part.

choices.text: Hold on to being a bird

effects.log: You go back to the bamboo groves and the sweet springs and the high ridge, and do the ordinary things, gathering, drinking, singing. It slows the change. It does not stop it. You did not really want it to.

choices.text: Ask your mate whether they feel it too

effects.log: "Since the spring," your mate says. "I did not want to say." You sit on the branch together and feel the land breathing under you, both of you, the whole long night.

events.text: People have started saying it: when a year is good, when the harvest comes in and nobody is hanged and the magistrate is fair and the children are fat, they call it the Phoenix's year. The grandmothers say it first. Then the farmers. Then, one spring, a ruler says it in a proclamation, and you hear it read out in a square and feel it land in you like a seed.

choices.text: Let it be your name now

effects.log: It is your name now, more than any title a court ever gave you. In a thousand villages, every good year, somebody says it. You feel every one.

choices.text: Visit the ruler who said it, unseen, and see if it is true

effects.log: You watch the court a season. The granaries are open. The prisons are nearly empty. The music is true. It is the Phoenix's year after all, and you had nothing to do with it, and that is exactly what it means.

events.text: Long into the last shape, the Qilin comes to the paulownia where you sleep, for the first time ever coming down instead of waiting above, and stands under the branch without bending the grass. "I came to see how it feels," it says. "To be peace and not to bring it. Will you tell me?"

choices.text: Tell it: like a slope at sunrise that has stopped waiting

effects.log: The Qilin listens with its head low and its soft horn almost touching the grass. "Then I will not take that shape," it says at last. "I would miss the waiting." It walks away into the morning, and the grass behind it does not even know it was there.

choices.text: Let it sit in the tree with you a night instead

effects.log: A qilin in a paulownia is a very strange sight, and the village below is talking about it for a hundred years. In the morning it climbs down carefully, and says, "Oh," and nothing else, and goes back up to heaven thinking.

events.text: A war is starting in the north: two kingdoms, an old border, a young king on each side with something to prove. The kind of war that eats a generation. A hundred years ago you would have flown over the camps and sung. Now you are not sure what you are, or what you would do.

choices.text: Do nothing, and see what peace does by itself

effects.log: You stay in the paulownia. In the north, the two young kings meet at the border to sign the declaration, and both of them, at the same moment, look up at a five-coloured sunrise and lose the thread of what they were going to say. It is a short war, and then it is not a war.

choices.text: Fly over the camps and sing, as you used to

effects.log: You sing over both camps at dusk, the old way, a bird. The truce lasts a night, then a year, then a reign. Some things are still better done with wings.

choices.text: Go to both kings in their tents at night and simply be seen

effects.log: Each king wakes in the night and finds a phoenix on the tent pole, looking at him. Neither says a word about it to anyone. Both of them, in the morning, find reasons to wait.

events.text: A thousand-year morning. Every land under heaven is quiet at once, which has never happened, and will not happen again for a long time. The paulownias on every slope are in leaf. The bamboo is not flowering anywhere. No ruler is cruel this year, by chance, or by something that is not chance. You could spread yourself over all of it, and stop being a bird.

choices.text: Become the peace

effects.log: You spread your five-coloured tail over the morning and the morning keeps it. You are no longer a bird that appears in peace. You are the peace. When a land is quiet, its people call it the Phoenix's year, and on the best of those mornings, someone in it looks up and sees two birds at sunrise.

choices.text: Stay a bird a little longer

effects.log: You fold your tail, and gather seed in an ordinary grove, and drink at an ordinary spring. The thousand-year morning goes by. There will be others. Not many. Enough.

events.text: You have not been back to the Cinnabar Cave since you left it as a drab, loud chick. Now, flying south over the mountain of gold and jade, you find you have come down at its mouth without deciding to. Inside, the red sand is smooth. There is a hollow in it about the size of an egg. It is warm.

choices.text: Go in and sit by the hollow

effects.log: You sit in the dark by the warm hollow and remember everything at once: the sand, the dance with no audience, the first song, the sparrow and its millet, the owl and its rat. It is a long remembering. When you come out it is spring.

choices.text: Sing and dance by yourself at the cave mouth, as you did

effects.log: You sing and dance by yourself, to nobody, because nobody is needed, the first steps you ever learned. You are very old and the steps are very young and they fit anyway.

choices.text: Fly on. The cave is for eggs

effects.log: You fly on south. But you look back once, and the cave mouth is glowing faintly in the dusk, like a coal that has stopped burning.

events.text: The warm hollow in the cave's red sand is warmer every time you pass. Now, from somewhere very far off, in another cave on another mountain, you can hear it: an egg, listening. You are suddenly sure that heaven would take you back to the beginning, if you asked, and let you keep everything you know.

choices.text: Ask the sky, plainly, whether that is so

effects.log: The sky does not answer in words. But the hollow in the sand, when you look again, is exactly your size, and there are no hoofprints at the cave mouth, and nobody is stopping you.

choices.text: Tell the far-off egg, in a song, that it is not alone

effects.log: You sing toward the other mountain. Very faintly, from inside a shell, something answers: a song turned the other way round. It is the first thing it has ever heard. It will spend a long time finding you.

events.text: You come down into the Cinnabar Cave one last time and lie down in the warm hollow in the red sand, just to see. It fits. The cave is very quiet. Below, the Cinnabar River runs south, as it always has. The sand begins, very gently, to close over you like a shell.

choices.text: Shake off the sand and fly out

effects.log: You shake off the sand and burst out of the cave mouth into the dusk, very loud, very much alive, a drab chick's hatching cry in a great bird's throat. The river below hears it. Not yet. Not this life.

choices.text: Let it close

effects.log: It closes. Heaven sends you back to the red sand of the cave, an egg again, the colour of a coal that has stopped burning, remembering everything. Somewhere far off, another egg is listening. This time you know it is there.

events.text: The first hall is the hall of Virtue, and it is full of the court you graced for virtue: the ruler, the ministers, the farmers who paid the tax, the guards who did not take bribes, all of them long dead, all standing in the cloud as they were on the day you came down in the dance. The ruler bows to you. Behind the ruler, a prisoner in a cangue, from that same reign, does not.

choices.text: Go to the prisoner first

effects.log: The prisoner tells you about the one cruelty in a good reign, the one you did not see. You listen. The pattern on your head does not dim; it grows, oddly, deeper.

choices.text: Walk the hall end to end and leave without a word

effects.log: You walk the hall of Virtue end to end in silence. At the far door you look back, and every face in it is turned toward you, and the pattern on your head is the same colour as the light in the doorway.

choices.text: Ask the Qilin, who walks behind you, what the hall is for

effects.log: "So you remember that it was people," says the Qilin. "Not a pattern. Not a reign. People, in a hall of Virtue, waiting for a bird."

events.text: The second hall is the hall of Righteousness: a court that went to war for a just cause, and won, and was generous after. The soldiers are here, all of them, the living and the dead, in their rows. The dead ones are looking at you very steadily.

choices.text: Bow to the dead soldiers first

effects.log: You bow to the dead rows. They do not bow back; they are soldiers. But the youngest one, at the end of a row, grins at you, as if you had passed something.

choices.text: Walk the hall end to end and leave without a word

effects.log: You walk the hall of Righteousness end to end in silence. At the far door you look back, and every face in it is turned toward you, and the pattern on your wings is the same colour as the light in the doorway.

choices.text: Ask the Qilin, who walks behind you, what the hall is for

effects.log: "So you remember that it was people," says the Qilin. "Not a pattern. Not a reign. People, in a hall of Righteousness, waiting for a bird."

events.text: The third hall is the hall of Propriety: a court of music and ceremony, every rite done right, every robe the proper colour, every bow the proper depth. It is very beautiful. It is also very still. A child at the back is trying not to fidget.

choices.text: Go and stand by the fidgeting child

effects.log: You stand by the child, who looks up at you and fidgets harder, delighted. Propriety, you realise, was always for the child, so that the child would grow up somewhere safe. The pattern on your back warms.

choices.text: Walk the hall end to end and leave without a word

effects.log: You walk the hall of Propriety end to end in silence. At the far door you look back, and every face in it is turned toward you, and the pattern on your back is the same colour as the light in the doorway.

choices.text: Ask the Qilin, who walks behind you, what the hall is for

effects.log: "So you remember that it was people," says the Qilin. "Not a pattern. Not a reign. People, in a hall of Propriety, waiting for a bird."

events.text: The fourth hall is the hall of Benevolence: a ruler who opened the granaries in a famine year and kept them open until the grain ran out, and then opened the palace storerooms. The hall smells of rice porridge. The ruler is ladling it out, still.

choices.text: Take a bowl, and do not eat it, and stand in the line

effects.log: You stand in the line with the bowl. The ruler ladles porridge into it without looking up, as for anybody. You carry it to the end of the hall and give it to a woman with two children, and the pattern on your breast shines.

choices.text: Walk the hall end to end and leave without a word

effects.log: You walk the hall of Benevolence end to end in silence. At the far door you look back, and every face in it is turned toward you, and the pattern on your breast is the same colour as the light in the doorway.

choices.text: Ask the Qilin, who walks behind you, what the hall is for

effects.log: "So you remember that it was people," says the Qilin. "Not a pattern. Not a reign. People, in a hall of Benevolence, waiting for a bird."

events.text: The fifth hall is the hall of Trust: a regent who held a throne for a child for twenty years and gave it back on the child's coming of age, to the day, with the seals and the treasury and the army, and went home to farm. The regent is here, old, with a hoe.

choices.text: Ask the regent why

effects.log: "I said I would," says the regent, puzzled that anyone would ask. Then, after a while: "And because I knew a bird was watching." The pattern on your belly warms like a hand.

choices.text: Walk the hall end to end and leave without a word

effects.log: You walk the hall of Trust end to end in silence. At the far door you look back, and every face in it is turned toward you, and the pattern on your belly is the same colour as the light in the doorway.

choices.text: Ask the Qilin, who walks behind you, what the hall is for

effects.log: "So you remember that it was people," says the Qilin. "Not a pattern. Not a reign. People, in a hall of Trust, waiting for a bird."

events.text: Past the fifth hall there is a sixth door, and it has no colour, and nobody has walked through it. The hoofprints on the floor stop in front of it. The Qilin stops with them. "That is the hall of a reign that has not happened yet," it says. "Whoever makes it will be the one you come for next. It is empty until then. Do you want to look?"

choices.text: Look

effects.log: It is a hall of cloud, empty, and very large, and the floor is swept. That is all. Somebody has swept it already, in hope. You stand in it a long time and then go out, and the Qilin, waiting, does not ask what you saw.

choices.text: Do not look. Let it be a surprise

effects.log: "Good," says the Qilin. "I never look either." You walk back through the five halls together, past the faces, and at the first door the Qilin says, almost shyly, that it has always wondered what a surprise feels like.

events.text: An envoy of the Jade court has come to audit the Four Spirits, as it audits the four guardians: every coming accounted for, every reign, every land. It has a retinue of clerks and a ledger bound in yellow silk. The Tortoise produces its shell. The Qilin produces nothing, since it walks without leaving any mark. The envoy turns to you, and asks the question it was sent to ask: "Why did heaven's omen come to that king?"

choices.text: Ask which king

effects.log: The envoy consults the ledger. The ledger has a long list. The envoy reads it aloud, king by king, for nine days, and at each one you answer, and the clerks run out of ink twice.

choices.text: Show the envoy the land itself, from the edge of heaven

effects.log: You take the envoy to the edge and show it the land below: the paulownias in their villages, the springs, the schoolhouses, the graves of the worthy. The envoy stops writing halfway through and simply looks.

choices.text: Lay a feather on the ledger, and say nothing

effects.log: One long five-coloured feather across the open page. The envoy looks at it a long time. Then it writes, very carefully, under the question: Answered.

events.text: The audit goes on for years, and comes at last to the false omens, if there were any, and the missed reigns, of which there were some, because there always are. The clerks have a separate ledger for these, bound in white hemp, and they handle it as if it were cold.

choices.text: Answer for every line in the white ledger

effects.log: You answer for each one: the reign you lent heaven to, the sage you were too far away to see. The envoy writes your answers in the white ledger in its own hand, not a clerk's, and at the end closes it gently, like a door on a sickroom.

choices.text: Ask the Tortoise to read it, since it keeps the record

effects.log: The tortoise reads it slowly. The serpent reads it fast. They argue about one line for a week. The envoy, by the end, has stopped being an auditor and become an audience.

events.text: The audit is concluded. The envoy is packing its ledgers, and it shows you, before it closes the yellow book, the last line it wrote on your page: Came, when asked by the worthy. Left, when it was time. Answered.

choices.text: Ask who audits the Jade court

effects.log: The envoy goes very still. The clerks stop packing. The Tortoise, to everyone's surprise, laughs out loud with both heads. The envoy leaves an hour early.

choices.text: Give the envoy a feather, for the road

effects.log: The envoy accepts it, with the expression of someone who will be asked about it for a thousand years. It is entered in the ledger: Feather, one. Received.

events.text: A ghost on your branch at dawn, thin as the steam off a rice pot: an old scholar in a horsehair hat, an exile from a reign you never came to, because you were in another land. "The phoenix does not come," he says, quite conversationally, "and the river gives no chart. I am finished. That is what I said. I thought you should hear it from me."

choices.text: Come down in the measured dance for him, here, now

effects.log: You dance for a ghost on a bare hill at dawn, centuries late. He watches the whole of it with his hands in his sleeves. At the end he nods, once, satisfied, like a teacher, and is not there. (-4 health)

choices.text: Tell him where you were, and why

effects.log: He listens. "A good reason," he says. "There is always a good reason. That is the trouble with omens." He is gone before you can answer, and you sit with that a long time.

choices.text: Ask him what he would have done if you had come

effects.log: "Nothing different," he says, surprised. "I only would have known." He looks at you as if that ought to be obvious. Then he fades, and the branch is wet with dew where he sat.

events.text: Scholars of the capital have built a shrine to an old sage who died in exile believing heaven had given up on the world. On the shrine's lintel, carved in large characters: the phoenix does not come. Every scholar who passes bows to it. They have made a virtue out of your absence.

choices.text: Sit on the lintel, over the characters, at the spring rite

effects.log: The rite stops. Two hundred scholars in their best robes look up at a five-coloured bird sitting on the words the phoenix does not come. Nobody knows what to do. The youngest scholar starts to laugh, and then, one by one, so do the rest, and then they all weep.

choices.text: Leave it. They need the absence more than the bird

effects.log: You leave it. A lintel that says you never came has made more honest scholars, you suspect, than you ever could by coming.

events.text: A human who stands at your level, which almost no human does: {npc}, an immortal of a great age, who has climbed to the edge of heaven on foot. {He} asks for nothing: no blessing, no feather, no omen. "Only the duet," {he} says. "Once. I heard it from a valley when I was nine, and I have wanted to hear it close all my life."
events.arc: Guests at the Edge of Heaven

choices.text: Sing it with your mate, close, for {him}

mem.note: heard the phoenixes' duet up close

effects.log: The duet goes wrong in the middle and right at the end. {npc} sits through all of it with {his} eyes shut, and at the end does not open them for a long time. "The middle," {he} says at last. "I never knew about the middle."

choices.text: Sing both halves alone, for {him}

mem.note: heard the lone phoenix sing both halves

effects.log: You sing both halves. {npc} understands at once what that means, and bows very low, not to you, to the empty place beside you.

choices.text: Sing one note, and let {him} imagine the rest

effects.log: One note, held. {npc} listens to it until it is gone, and then laughs. "That is better," {he} says. "Now I can never be disappointed."

events.text: An envoy of the Jade court, {npc}, in plain clothes, on your branch at dusk, travelling ahead of an audit. "Off the record," {he} says, "why did heaven's omen once come to a king with a crime under the throne? The court wants to know whether the Phoenix can be fooled."
events.arc: Guests at the Edge of Heaven

choices.text: Tell {him} the truth: yes, it can

effects.log: {npc} writes it down, and then puts the brush down. "Thank you," {he} says. "The court was afraid the answer would be no."

choices.text: Tell {him} that is why there are four of you

effects.log: "The Qilin asks," you say. "The Tortoise records. The Dragon listens. I come. Any one of us can be fooled. All four, less often." {npc} looks at you a long time and says that it is the best answer to an audit question that {he} has ever heard.

choices.text: Ask {him} whether the Jade court can be fooled

effects.log: {npc} goes very still. Then {he} laughs, quietly, and gets up off your branch. "Off the record," {he} says, "often."

events.text: An immortal sovereign, {npc}, ruler of a court in the high heavens, has come in person, with a retinue, to ask for a pair of phoenixes on {his} palace roof. Not a blessing; a decoration. "I have the finest paulownias in the heavens," {he} says. "A spring that tastes of rice wine. Bamboo that flowers every year, by my order."
events.arc: Guests at the Edge of Heaven

choices.text: Decline, and fly

effects.log: {npc} does not take no. For a century {his} court's messengers turn up on your branch with better offers. For a century you fly. In the end {he} has two birds carved on the roof instead, and pretends that was what {he} wanted.

choices.text: Ask whether bamboo that flowers by order is still bamboo

effects.log: {npc} opens {his} mouth, and shuts it. {His} retinue look at the floor. "It dies every year," {he} admits at last. "The whole grove. We replant it." {He} goes home thoughtful, and the next year {his} bamboo is left alone.

choices.text: Watch {his} court for a season first, as you would any

effects.log: You watch the court in the high heavens a season, unseen, the granaries and the prisons and the music. You do not come. {npc} understands exactly why, and never asks again, and is, after that, slightly better.

events.text: A heavenly immortal stops you at the door of cloud: {npc}, who bows very low. "You will not remember me," {he} says. "Long ago I was a child on a farm whose family planted a paulownia the year I was born. A bird sat in it every morning. I talked to it every morning. When it was cut for my wedding chest I asked the bird what to do."
events.arc: Guests at the Edge of Heaven

choices.text: Say you remember

mem.note: was the child of the paulownia, remembered by the Phoenix

effects.log: You do: the farmyard, the morning voice, the axe. {npc} weeps, and then laughs, and asks what you told {him} back then. You tell {him}. {He} says it was the right answer, and that {he} did the other thing anyway, and it was also right.

choices.text: Ask what became of the chest

mem.note: told the Phoenix about the wedding chest

effects.log: "A stranger painted a bird on the lid," says {npc}. "The stranger had never seen one. So I painted the second bird myself. The chest is in a descendant's house still, generations on, and they argue about which bird is which."

events.text: A ruler of the land below, {npc}, has climbed the mountain alone, without guards, which rulers never do. "I know you have been watching me," {he} says to the paulownia. "Three seasons. The granaries and the prisons. I would like to know what you saw. Not whether you will come. Only what you saw."
events.arc: Guests at the Edge of Heaven

choices.text: Tell {him} everything, the good and the bad

effects.log: {npc} listens to all of it, the good granary in the west and the bad prison in the east, without defending anything. Then {he} goes down the mountain and closes the prison in the east, and does not tell anyone why.

choices.text: Ask {him} what {he} thinks you saw

effects.log: {npc} tells you. It is harder on {him} than you would have been. You say nothing. {He} nods, as if you had agreed, and goes down the mountain to mend the worst of it.

choices.text: Say nothing. Rulers who climb mountains alone are already being seen

effects.log: You say nothing. {npc} waits until dusk, then bows to the empty branch, and goes down. The heralds do not hear of it. The people do, somehow, and like {him} better.

events.text: A sect master of the murim, {npc}, at the head of a hundred disciples in matching robes, has come to your mountain with banners. "Bless our sect," {he} says, "and we will paint you on every gate in the south. You are the omen. We would be the omen's sect."
events.arc: Guests at the Edge of Heaven

choices.text: Refuse: you are no one's

effects.log: {npc} goes red, then white. The disciples look at their feet. On the way down the mountain, three of them quietly leave the sect, which you did not intend, and do not regret.

choices.text: Watch the sect a season before you answer

effects.log: You watch: the training yard, the punishment hall, the way the senior disciples treat the juniors. You do not come. The sect paints you on its gates anyway, and the juniors, who know you watched, learn to look up at the painting with a very particular expression.

choices.text: Ask {him} to tell you, first, what the sect has done for the poor

effects.log: {npc} starts to answer, and stops, and starts again. It is a short answer. {He} goes down the mountain without the blessing, and the next year the sect opens a free clinic at its gate, and the year after, {he} climbs back up to tell you about it.

events.text: A grandmaster of the murim, {npc}, has come to fight you. Not out of malice: {he} is the best under heaven and has heard that the Phoenix does not strike first, and wants to know what that means, from inside. "Strike second, then," {he} says, and bows, and raises {his} sword.
events.arc: Guests at the Edge of Heaven

choices.text: Let {him} strike first, and answer

ok.log: {He} strikes first. You answer with the high branch and the morning sun and a voice from the ridge. When it is over {npc} sits on the rock with a broken sword, laughing. "Second," {he} says. "Second is a whole other art."

fail.log: {npc} is better than anyone has a right to be. You fly off the duel with a cut along your wing. {He} bows to the sky after you, pleased. (-15 health)

choices.text: Fly off the duel before it starts

effects.log: You rise off the branch. {npc} lowers the sword, and watches you go, and says to nobody: "Ah. So that is what it means." {He} goes home and does not draw a sword in anger for the rest of {his} life.

choices.text: Sit still on the branch and wait for {him} to strike

effects.log: {npc} raises the sword, and holds it, and holds it, and cannot bring it down on a bird that is only sitting there looking at {him}. At dusk {he} sheathes it. "That," {he} says, "was the hardest fight of my life."

events.text: A painter of the old folk style, {npc}, has climbed your slope with paper and five pots of colour. {He} has painted the red sun and the paulownia and a pair of phoenixes a thousand times for wedding screens, and never once seen one. "I always paint two," {he} says, "because the customers want two. Tell me honestly: is it wrong?"
events.arc: Guests at the Edge of Heaven

choices.text: Tell {him} it is right: there are always two

effects.log: {npc} paints for a week, a red sun, a paulownia, a bird, and then, with great care, a second long tail trailing in from the edge of the paper, the bird itself out of sight. "There," {he} says. It is the best painting {he} ever makes.

choices.text: Sit for {him}, one bird, all day

effects.log: {npc} paints one bird for the first time in {his} life, slowly, all day. At dusk {he} looks at it and says it looks lonely. Then {he} looks at you, and says, quite kindly, that it does not, really.

events.text: A farmer from the village under the ridge, {npc}, climbs to your paulownia with a bowl of millet. "I know you will not eat it," {he} says. "I only wanted to give you something. My old partner at the plough used to say that when the birds sang on the ridge the farm would be all right. They are gone now. You still sing. I wanted to say thank you."
events.arc: Guests at the Edge of Heaven

choices.text: Sing for {him}, now, the morning song

effects.log: You sing the morning song on the branch over the bowl of millet. {npc} listens to it standing up, and at the end sits down on the roots of the paulownia and stays there until noon, and goes home lighter.

choices.text: Take one grain, and hold it, and do not eat it

effects.log: One grain in your beak, held, and set down again on the branch beside you. {npc} understands. It is the only time in all your years that you have accepted millet, and nobody but the two of you will ever know.

events.text: A geomancer, {npc}, smooth-voiced and well dressed, has come to your mountain from the capital. "The king would like to build you something," {he} says. "Mounds. Round ones. Eggs, of a kind, all over the city, so that you will feel at home and never leave."
events.arc: Guests at the Edge of Heaven

choices.text: Tell {him} plainly that you will leave when you must, eggs or not

effects.log: {npc} smiles and bows and goes. The mounds are not built. Years later you learn that {he} was paid by a rival kingdom, and that your answer cost {him} a very great deal of money.

choices.text: Ask {him} who is paying {him}

effects.log: {npc} stops smiling. {He} looks at you a long while. "Somebody who knows how birds think," {he} says, "and how kings think about birds." {He} leaves that night, and the capital never hears of the eggs.

events.text: Drums in the capital: a new ruler holds the land below. The heralds say heaven smiles on the reign. They always say that. They have painted two birds on the coronation banners without asking, and the ceremony is waiting, very slightly, to see whether a real one will turn up.

choices.text: Stay away. You have not watched this one yet

effects.log: You stay away. The ceremony waits an hour longer than it should, and then goes on without you, and the new ruler notes it, and wonders. (Watch the Court before you come.)

choices.text: Fly over the ceremony high, without stopping

effects.log: Everyone sees you go over, high, toward somewhere else. The heralds say it was a blessing. The old people say it was a bird going about its business. Both are right.

choices.text: Go and look at the granaries before the feast

effects.log: While the court feasts you are on the granary roof, counting sacks. It is too soon to tell. But the new ruler has kept on the old granary-keeper, which is something.

events.text: A new ruler below, and this one sends a letter up the mountain before the coronation: no gifts, no millet, no cage. It says only that the new reign will try to deserve you, and asks you not to come until it does.

choices.text: Keep the letter in the nest

effects.log: You keep it in the nest, under the down. You read it twice, and decide this one may be worth watching. (Watch the Court.)

choices.text: Fly over the palace once, so they know it was received

effects.log: One pass over the palace at dusk, low and slow. The new ruler is on the terrace, alone, and bows. You do not come down. Not yet.

events.text: A new ruler below, and the springs know before you do: the one under the palace wall, which went dry in the last reign, has started to flow again in the night. The palace servants are carrying the news up and down the city in buckets.

choices.text: Go and taste it

effects.log: Sweet. Not the sweetest you have tasted, but sweet, and clean, and getting sweeter. You fly home in a good mood, which your mate notices and does not mention. (Watch the Court to be sure.)

choices.text: Do not trust it yet. Springs have been wrong

effects.log: You stay away from the spring and watch the prisons instead. They are emptying, slowly. The spring was not wrong. Not this time.

events.text: A new ruler below, and from the edge of heaven it is very small: one more name, one more coronation, one more reign of ten or forty years in a land you have watched for a thousand. The Qilin, walking beside you on the cloud, asks whether you still look.

choices.text: "Every time"

effects.log: "Good," says the Qilin. "The day you stop, they will feel it." You fly down the light to watch the granaries, as you did when you were young.

choices.text: "Less than I did"

effects.log: The Qilin nods. "So do I," it says. "That is why we go down anyway." You go down together, and watch the new court for a season from a temple roof, a phoenix and a qilin, and nobody notices either of you.

events.text: The palace spring tastes of iron. You noticed it at dawn and hoped you were wrong. The ruler you came in the dance for is old now, and frightened, and has begun to listen to the wrong people. Two ministers who argued with the throne are in the prison you once saw nearly empty.

choices.text: Taste it again, carefully, to be sure

effects.log: Iron, and something under the iron, bitter. You are sure. (The reign you graced is declining. Leave the Land before your pattern dulls.)

choices.text: Ask your mate what they taste

effects.log: "Iron," says your mate at once, and then, gently: "Since the spring. I was waiting for you to taste it." (Leave the Land before your pattern dulls.)

choices.text: Stay one more season. Old rulers recover

effects.log: One more season. The iron does not go out of the water. A third minister goes into the prison. (Leave the Land before your pattern dulls.)

events.text: The heir to the reign you graced has come of age, and the court is already calling the heir heaven's chosen, because heaven chose the parent, and the Phoenix came. The heir has a cold eye and a long list of names. The palace spring has begun, very faintly, to taste of iron.

choices.text: Watch the heir yourself before you decide

effects.log: A season over the heir's household. Cruel to the servants, sweet to the ministers, patient in a way that frightens you. The spring is right. (Leave the Land before your pattern dulls.)

choices.text: Let the court say what it likes. You came for the parent

effects.log: You let it be. In the villages they say the Phoenix blessed the heir too. You did not. It does not matter, to the villages. (Leave the Land before your pattern dulls.)

events.text: Still in the land you graced, and the reign rotting under you. The pattern it gave you aches, the way an old bone aches in the rain. The people below have started to look up at you on the palace roof with a look you have not seen before: not hope, not fear. A question.

choices.text: Answer it: go up to the roof ridge at noon

effects.log: You climb to the ridge of the palace roof at noon, where everyone can see. (Leave the Land: the people are waiting for it.)

choices.text: Look away from them

effects.log: You look away. The question does not go away. It gets louder, every year you stay, until it is not a question any more.

events.text: The court below is playing the old music, and you are ready to come down in the dance. Your mate, beside you on the ridge-tile, has not moved. "Not this one," they say. "I have watched it as long as you have. I do not care what the granaries look like. I do not trust the face."

choices.text: Trust them, and do not come

effects.log: You fold your wings. The music plays to the end without you, and the ruler looks up at an empty sky, and you do not know, yet, whether your mate was right. You may never know. That is the price of a pair.

choices.text: Argue it out on the roof all night

effects.log: All night, in low voices, on the ridge-tile. The granaries, the prisons, the face. By dawn neither of you has moved the other an inch, but you each know exactly why the other thinks what they think, which is something.

choices.text: Tell them gently that you will go, and that they need not follow

effects.log: "I always follow," they say, "and you always know that." (Come in the Dance, if you still mean to.)

events.text: Your mate was right about this reign. They said it was not worthy. You overruled them, and came, and it was a false omen, and the villages learned to spit at painted birds. They have never once mentioned it. Tonight, on the branch, you find you want them to.

choices.text: Say it first: you were right

effects.log: "I know," says your mate, and then, after a long time: "I wish I had not been." You sit closer than you have in a century.

choices.text: Say nothing, and sit closer

effects.log: You say nothing. Your mate says nothing. The branch creaks under the two of you. That is the whole conversation, and it is enough.

events.text: The seed store is empty, even now, even at your age. A thousand years and you still have not learned to keep enough. A sparrow lands beside you with a grain of millet in its beak, out of kindness, the way a sparrow did when you were a drab, loud chick.

choices.text: Thank it, and fast

effects.log: "A thousand li hungry," you tell the sparrow. It has heard that before, from your kind. It stays with you on the branch anyway, all the cold day, for company. (-10 health)

choices.text: Take the grain

effects.log: You take it. It tastes of nothing you want, and the sparrow looks at you with an expression you do not like at all. (-8 purity)

choices.text: Let your mate give you their share

effects.log: Your mate pushes the last of their seed toward you along the branch and says they are not hungry. You both know they are. You eat. You will remember the winter. (The mate grows thinner.)

variants: Empty again: the oldest phoenix under heaven, and the seed store bare as a chick's. A sparrow lands beside you with one grain of millet in its beak, exactly as a sparrow once did when you were small and loud and drab.

A thousand years of winters, and still the store runs out. A sparrow settles on your branch and lays a single grain of millet by your foot, kindly, as its kind have done for yours since you were a chick.
The bamboo has not seeded, and the store is dust. A small brown sparrow hops along the branch to you with a grain of millet, out of plain kindness, as if you were still the drab chick it once fed.

events.text: A lean year, and the farmers below know it before you do: the bamboo along their streams has not flowered in a generation, and the bird on the ridge is thin. One morning there is a little heap of bamboo seed on a flat stone at the foot of your paulownia. Not millet. Bamboo seed, gathered by hand, grain by grain, from somewhere very far.

choices.text: Eat it, and sing them a morning in thanks

effects.log: You eat it. It was gathered right; somebody asked somebody old how. You sing the village a morning it remembers for a generation.

choices.text: Leave it for a bird that needs it more, and fast

effects.log: You leave it. A young crane takes it, the next day, and the farmers are disappointed, and then, when they see the crane, not. (-10 health)

variants: A lean year, and the people below have noticed the thin bird on the ridge before you noticed yourself. At dawn there is a little heap on the flat stone under your paulownia: bamboo seed, not millet, gathered grain by grain from groves a long way off.

events.text: The Lean Year, at the edge of heaven. Up here there is no bamboo, no millet, no farmyard, no sparrow. Only light, and the old hunger, which it turns out has followed you all the way up.

choices.text: Fly down to the groves and search, hungry

effects.log: Down the light to the world, hungry, and a whole season in the groves for one handful. It is enough for the year, barely. (-6 health)

choices.text: Fast in the light

effects.log: You fast in the light. It does not feed you. It does something else, which is almost as good, and you come out of the year thinner and clearer. (-10 health)

events.text: Word on the wind, from bird to bird: the bamboo of a far province is in flower. All of it, all at once, for the first time in sixty years. You have seen a dozen of these now. You know what comes after: the grove dies, the rats swarm on the fallen seed, and then on the granaries.

choices.text: Gather your store, and go

effects.log: You gather enough for a decade and leave the rest. (Gather Bamboo Seed while the flowering lasts.)

choices.text: Warn the villages: fill the granaries, keep cats, build rat-walls

effects.log: You fly over every village in the province calling. Some of them understand; old people remember their grandparents' stories. The rats come anyway. Fewer people starve than in the last flowering, and some of the old people say why.

choices.text: Gather, and leave a share at the village granaries

effects.log: Half for you, half poured on the threshing floors of the poorest villages at night. Bamboo seed is not rice, but it is food, and in the rat year it is the difference.

events.text: The bamboo is flowering in a province below, and your mate wants to go and gather together, as you did the very first time, a thousand years ago, when the seed fell like rain and you were young and did not know about the rats.

choices.text: Go together, as you did

effects.log: A season in the flowering grove, the two of you, the seed falling on your backs. You do not talk about the rats. You both know. You both gather anyway, and it is, for a season, exactly like being young.

choices.text: Go alone, and let your mate rest

effects.log: You gather for both. It takes twice as long. When you come back the nest is warm and your mate has been, without saying so, worried the whole time.

events.text: Feather-takers on your slope again: three of them, with poles, lime-sticks and a net weighted with lead. A single five-coloured tail feather sells for a year's rice to the crown-makers of the hill kingdoms, and the old trade has never quite died.

choices.text: Fly high and stay there until they give up

effects.log: Three days at the height of the cranes. They give up on the fourth, and leave the lime-sticks, which you knock into the stream.

choices.text: Let them see you, close, and look at them

effects.log: You land on a branch at the height of their eyes and look at them. Nobody raises a pole. The youngest of them goes home and takes up farming, and the others follow, in time.

choices.text: Lead them in circles until nightfall

ok.log: Up the valley, down the valley, round the lake twice. By nightfall they are lost and very tired and blaming each other. They go home with nothing.

fail.log: A lime-stick catches your tail on the last turn. You tear free and leave a feather, and the feather-takers go home with a year's rice and a very good story. (-8 health)

events.text: A cage-maker of the capital, famous for birdcages so fine the birds forget they are in them, has built one for you: bamboo, not gilt, with a paulownia perch and a basin for spring water. It is beautiful. It is on a hill under your tree with the door open. {npc} sits beside it, waiting, and does not hide.

choices.text: Ask {him} why

effects.log: "Because it is the best cage I will ever make," says {npc}, "and I wanted it to be for the best bird." {He} does not seem to think you will go in. {He} only wanted you to see it. You do. It is very good.

choices.text: Go in, look, and come out again

effects.log: You walk in, look at the perch and the basin and the light through the bamboo, and walk out. {npc} weeps with pride. {He} never builds another, and the cage hangs empty in {his} workshop, the most famous cage in the land.

choices.text: Break it

effects.log: You break it with one blow of a wing, and {npc} watches without moving. "Yes," {he} says. "That is the right thing to do with it." {He} goes home and sweeps up the pieces and keeps one.

events.text: A court physician with an armed escort has come up the mountain to buy, beg or take one of your eggs. The king is dying, and an old book says that a phoenix's egg, boiled in a sweet spring, cures every sickness. There is no egg. The physician does not believe you.

choices.text: Show the empty nest

effects.log: The physician looks into the empty nest a long time. Then the escort leaves, and the physician stays, and asks you, as one healer to something like a healer, what really might help. You do not know. You fly with the physician to the palace anyway.

choices.text: Drive off the escort

ok.log: The escort goes down the mountain faster than it came up. The physician stays, sitting on a rock, and laughs, a little hysterically, and says that it was a stupid book anyway.

fail.log: They have spears and you have no reason to strike first. You fly off with a cut on your leg. They search the nest, find nothing, and go home to a dying king. (-10 health)

events.text: A quiet century at the edge of heaven. Your mate has taken up counting the paulownias of the world from up here, one by one, and keeps losing count, and starting again, and enjoying it.

choices.text: Count with them

effects.log: You count together, and lose count together, and argue about whether that one was a paulownia or a plane tree. It takes a century. You never finish. It is one of the best centuries.

choices.text: Tell them the number is always changing

effects.log: "I know," your mate says. "That is why it is a good thing to count." They start again.

events.text: A quiet century, alone at the edge of heaven. You keep the vow. You sing both halves every dawn. Some mornings the second half comes easily, as if somebody were singing it with you. Some mornings it does not.

choices.text: Sing it anyway, both halves, every dawn

effects.log: Every dawn. The hard mornings and the easy ones. Below, in a hundred villages, people who wake early hear two voices from the sky and do not know that one of them is only remembered.

choices.text: Rest one morning, and let the silence be theirs

effects.log: One morning you do not sing. The silence where their half should be is enormous. Then a lark starts, far below, very badly, and you laugh, and sing after all.

events.text: An argument at the edge of heaven, the first in a hundred years: your mate thinks the paulownias in the eastern hills are being cut too fast, and wants to go down and do something. You think a phoenix does nothing; it only comes, or does not.

choices.text: Go down with them anyway

effects.log: You go down together and sit in the paulownias of the eastern hills for a season, in full sight. Nobody cuts a tree a phoenix is sitting in. By the time you leave, the hill villages have started planting again.

choices.text: Hold your ground: you only come

effects.log: Your mate goes down alone for a season. They come back with leaves in their tail and do not say how it went. The eastern hills are greener, a few years later, and they still do not say.

events.text: A good year in a land you have never even visited, a small kingdom in the far south-west. The harvest is in. The magistrate is fair. A grandmother on a threshing floor says it is the Phoenix's year, and you feel it, a thousand li away, like a warm hand on your back.

choices.text: Go and see it

effects.log: You go and see it: threshing floors, drying peppers on the roofs, a grandmother asleep in the sun. Nobody looks up. Nobody needs to.

choices.text: Stay where you are and feel it

effects.log: You stay. It is enough to know. The warm hand on your back stays all autumn.

events.text: A bad year somewhere: a flood, a cruel governor, a plague village. You feel that too, now, like a cold place on your breast. Peace is not only the good years. It is what the bad years are measured against.

choices.text: Go to the cold place, and be seen there

effects.log: You sit on the roof of the plague village's shrine for a season, in sight of everyone. You cannot cure anything. But the village stops dying of fear, which was half of it. (-6 health)

choices.text: Sing toward it from far off

effects.log: You sing from the edge of heaven toward the cold place. It does not warm. But in the plague village, a child who cannot sleep hears something very far off, and sleeps.

events.text: A wedding in a farming village: a chest of paulownia wood, two birds painted on its lid, one by a stranger who never saw a phoenix and one, clumsily, by the bride. You have seen this chest before, or one just like it, long ago. The bride's grandmother is telling the story of the tree.

choices.text: Land on the gatepost for the wedding

effects.log: The whole wedding stops. The bride looks at you, and at the two painted birds on her chest, and laughs out loud. The grandmother says she knew it. Every grandmother at every wedding in the land says it for a hundred years afterwards.

choices.text: Watch from the paulownia by the gate, unseen

effects.log: They plant a new paulownia by the gate the day of the wedding, for a daughter not yet born. You make a note of the tree.

events.text: The Tortoise climbs up to see you, which takes it eleven years, and both heads are complaining about the height. It has brought the record. "Nothing to report," says the tortoise. "For three centuries," says the serpent. "We have never had less to write," they finish together. "It is very boring. Thank you."

choices.text: Ask them to stay a while anyway

effects.log: They stay a decade. The serpent tells stories about the four directions. The tortoise corrects them. You have not laughed so much in a thousand years.

choices.text: Ask to see the record

effects.log: Three centuries of the shell, and on each line in the tortoise's slow hand: A quiet year. The serpent has added, in the margin of one: Probably the bird.

events.text: The Yellow Dragon of the centre comes to the edge of heaven where you are, with the patience of farmland, and lies down beside you on the cloud without a word. It stays a year. At the end of the year it says only: "So this is what the centre was for."

choices.text: Ask what it means

effects.log: "The centre holds the four directions still," it says, "so that something like you can happen in the middle of them." Then it goes back to pretending to sleep, and you are not sure it was not asleep the whole time.

choices.text: Lie beside it another year, saying nothing

effects.log: Another year of nothing, beside the Yellow Dragon. It is, you think afterwards, the most restful year either of you has ever had. The land below has a very good harvest, and nobody knows why.
